    The outbreak of SARS-CoV-2 in China gave rise to a global pandemic with more than 20 million cases in July 2020. Many countries were or are still under lockdown, but this strategy is hard to maintain for extended periods due to its socioeconomic consequences. Mathematical modelling may help authorities to make informed decisions about possible strategies for safely lifting lockdown.

    We developed a mathematical model to assess the number of tests needed to identify all the infected individuals in Lusaka, Zambia, and to evaluate the impact of different testing strategies on the number of new infections during the first 14 days of the removal of restrictions.

    Depending on the testing strategy considered, 48%–100% of the individuals in Lusaka need to be tested to identify all infected individuals. To achieve a 90% reduction of new infections, we estimate that 48%–100% of the individuals in Lusaka need to be tested if only symptomatic individuals are tested, 75%–100% of the individuals need to be tested if only individuals with severe symptoms are tested, and 48%–99% of the individuals need to be tested if asymptomatic and pre-symptomatic individuals are also tested.

    Our results suggest that a blanket testing approach may offer a good strategy to control the outbreak if the testing capacity is available.

    This modelling study suggests that a high number of individuals in Lusaka, Zambia, need to be tested to control the outbreak and that the testing strategy is a crucial element for the success of the lifting of restrictions. Our results also suggest that a blanket testing approach may offer a good strategy to control the outbreak, but it should be combined with contact tracing and a ‘safe and healthy work’. The majority of the studies conducted in Africa have focused on the clinical characteristics of COVID-19 patients, with limited information on the proportion of asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic individuals. Here, we systematically reviewed the proportion of asymptomatic or mild COVID-19 cases reported in Africa. We found that the proportion of asymptomatic or mild COVID-19 cases ranged from 0 to 31% among the confirmed cases and from 0 to 66.7% among the exposed cases. The proportion of asymptomatic or mild cases was higher in studies that used serology testing as part of the case definition. There was limited evidence from Africa on the clinical characteristics of the early stage of COVID-19. More research is needed to define the clinical course of COVID-19 in Africa and to identify the risk factors for severe disease.

In this study, we examined the viral loads of asymptomatic individuals by using RT-PCR and RT-qPCR to detect SARS-CoV-2 RNA in oropharyngeal (OP) and nasal (NP) samples collected from a group of international asymptomatic individuals entering Japan between March and May 2020. The viral RNA was detected in 37.5% (12/32) of OP samples and 6.3% (2/32) of NP samples. The OP viral loads of the positive individuals were significantly higher than those of the NP samples (p<0.001). We also examined the relationship between viral loads and several factors, including age, sex, travel destination, and duration of stay overseas. The viral load in the OP samples was not associated with the duration of stay overseas, sex, or travel destination. However, a significant negative correlation was found between viral load and age, and younger individuals had higher viral loads than older individuals. These findings suggest that the OP samples of younger asymptomatic individuals who have recently returned from abroad may be an important source of SARS-CoV-2 infection. To prevent the spread of COVID-19, it is important to develop a screening method that can identify individuals with a high viral load in the upper respiratory tract.

However, when asymptomatic individuals comprised 70% of all cases, the majority of secondary infections were acquired from the remaining 30% of individuals with symptoms, while when asymptomatic individuals comprised 50% of cases, the majority of secondary infections were acquired from the remaining 50% of individuals with symptoms. This suggests that to effectively reduce the number of secondary infections, it is important to isolate and treat a large proportion of individuals with symptoms. Our findings also suggest that if a large proportion of the population is asymptomatic, the number of secondary infections can still be reduced by isolating and treating a large proportion of individuals with symptoms. This is important because recent estimates suggest that a large proportion of the population may be asymptomatic. For example, in one study conducted in the Hubei province of China, 81.7% of COVID-19 patients were asymptomatic. In another study, researchers estimated that 96% of all COVID-19 cases in Wuhan were asymptomatic. However, because the number of asymptomatic individuals is not known, it is difficult to determine the proportion of the population that needs to be isolated and treated to effectively reduce the number of secondary infections. Therefore, more research is needed to estimate the proportion of individuals who are asymptomatic. The first scenario is relevant for the early stages of an outbreak when the majority of cases are symptomatic and the second scenario is relevant for the later stages of an outbreak when a large proportion of cases are asymptomatic.

The model was fitted to data from the current COVID-19 pandemic in the United States. Specifically, the model was fitted to data from the state of New York (NY) which has been the epicenter of the pandemic in the United States. The model was fitted to data from March 25th to May 22nd, 2020, which is the period when the majority of COVID-19 deaths in the state of NY occurred. The model was fitted to age specific death rates and the age specific prevalence of cases which were obtained from the New York State Department of Health. The fitted model was used to simulate the number of COVID-19 deaths in New York if the state had not implemented a lockdown.

The model was also fitted to data from the current COVID-19 pandemic in South Africa. The model was fitted to the daily new cases and daily new deaths from May 1st to June 10th, 2020. The model was fitted to the new data using the estimated parameters from the New York data. The fitted model was used to simulate the number of COVID-19 deaths in South Africa if the country had not implemented a lockdown.

(2020)

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused more than 1.2 million deaths globally and infected over 56 million people across the world, according to the latest data from Johns Hopkins University. While the number of cases in the United States and Europe has come down in recent weeks, the situation is worsening in Latin America and parts of Africa. India has also seen a recent spurt in cases.

Lockdowns, social distancing, and the use of masks have become the new normal in most countries. But with the number of cases expected to rise in many countries in the coming months, health experts are looking at other ways to contain the spread of the virus.

Mass testing is one such method that many experts believe can help keep the pandemic in check. But implementing mass testing is easier said than done, and experts point out that it is also not a magic solution to end the pandemic.

We asked experts to tell us about the pros and cons of mass testing and how it has been done in different countries.

What is mass testing?

Mass testing means conducting tests for a large number of people in a short period of time. The aim is to identify as many people who could be infected and put them under quarantine or isolation.

“Mass testing is a public health strategy that aims to identify people who are infected with an infectious disease, and separate them from those who are not,” says Dr. Shuba Singhal, a pediatrician and member of the National Task Force on COVID-19 in India.

The strategy is used to control the spread of infectious diseases. “It is a key control strategy for infectious diseases like COVID-19, tuberculosis, and cholera,” says Dr. Akshay Nayar, an internal medicine specialist at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and CEO of 1doc.com, an online platform that connects patients with doctors.

Mass testing is different from testing a representative sample of the population. The latter is a scientific method used to draw broad inferences about a given population based on a small sample of the population.

For instance, a public health agency may decide to test 1,000 people to understand the extent of polio in a population of 10 million. This method is used to estimate the prevalence of a disease in a community.

On the other hand, mass testing is not done to estimate the prevalence of a disease, but to identify as many people who are infected with the disease as possible. It is also done to isolate those who are infected from those who are not.

To investigate the genetic architecture of complex traits in African populations, we analyzed whole-genome sequence data from 2,756 Yoruban individuals without known shared ancestry from the African Biobank Initiative. We identified 48,162 high-confidence loss-of-function variants, of which 13,977 are rare (minor allele frequency <5%) and 34,185 are common (minor allele frequency ≥5%). We provide the most comprehensive catalog of loss-of-function variants to date in any population. We show that loss-of-function variants are partially depleted at the protein-coding loci implicated in complex trait-associated genes in Yorubans but not in European individuals from the 1000 Genomes Project. This result provides support for the purifying selection acting on complex trait-associated genes in sub-Saharan African populations. We also report that, in Yoruban individuals, the distributions of loss-of-function variants are significantly different between genes with and without associations with complex traits in African and non-African populations. Our findings contribute to an understanding of the genetic architecture of complex traits in Africans and highlight the importance of examining diverse populations.

The genetic basis of disease is complex and is influenced by many factors. For example, the risk of developing a genetic disease may depend on the frequency of the genetic variant in the population, the number of times a person carries the variant, the influence of the variant on the function of other genes, and the influence of a person’s environment.

Researchers have developed methods to predict whether a person has a genetic disease based on the person’s genetic information. These methods have been extensively tested in people of European ancestry but have not been tested in people of African ancestry.

Here, we present two case studies that illustrate the challenges in accurately predicting whether a person has a genetic disease based on their genetic information when the person is of African ancestry.

The first case study focuses on a genetic disease caused by two genetic variants that increase the risk of developing the disease when a person has both variants. The second case study focuses on a genetic disease caused by a common genetic variant that increases the risk of developing the disease when a person has two copies of the variant.

We show how the frequency of the genetic variants in the population influences the accuracy of the predictions. We also show how including information about a person’s environment can improve the accuracy of the predictions.

Finally, we end with a call to action to improve methods for predicting genetic disease risk in people of African ancestry.

Case study 1: Predicting sickle cell disease

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is caused by a genetic variant in the gene that provides instructions for making haemoglobin. The variant leads to the production of abnormal haemoglobin, which causes red blood cells to become rigid and deform into a sickle shape. The abnormally shaped cells can get stuck in blood vessels and reduce blood flow, causing pain and organ damage.

SCD is a rare disease in people of European ancestry but is common in people of African, Middle Eastern, and South American ancestry because similar genetic variants that increase the risk of developing SCD are more common in these populations.

A person needs to have two copies of the variant (one copy from each parent) to develop SCD. However, having one copy of the variant increases a person’s risk of developing other health problems, such as anaemia, infections, and stroke.

A team of researchers from the University of Washington, the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, and the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), all in the United States, showed that disease-associated genetic variants in African Americans are less likely than those of European descent to be tagged by methods that look for small changes in the DNA code. The work appears in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

“People of African descent in the United States and in other parts of the world have been systematically excluded from genetic research,” said Dr. Eimear McGuinness, assistant professor of pharmaceutics at the University of Washington School of Pharmacy. “This study shows that by excluding these individuals, the medical community may be missing a substantial number of genetic variants that could help predict disease risk,” she said in a university news release.

McGuinness and Dr. Namiko Reihaneh, an assistant professor of human genetics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, began the study by looking at the results of genome-wide association studies (GWAS). These are large analyses of many people’s genetic data to look for associations between specific genetic variants and disease.

The researchers then focused on 2,360 reported associations between genetic variants and disease risk that were identified in people of European descent. The team found that only 16% of these associations were replicated when the analysis was done in people of African descent — even when the researchers controlled for the number of variants tested and the number of individuals included in the analysis.

McGuinness and Reihaneh also found that most genetic variant-finding methods are designed using data from people of European descent. This means that when these methods are applied to people of African descent, they might be less effective at finding disease-associated genetic variants.

Dr. Drayton Gereau, assistant professor of psychiatry at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, said the study results “point to a critical gap in the translation of genomic medicine for African Americans.” He added that the findings “further highlight the importance of diverse datasets for discovering and validating genomic markers of disease.”

McGuinness said the new study doesn’t mean that genetic testing isn’t useful for people of African descent. “It just means that we need to be very thoughtful about the design and the interpretation of these tests,” she explained.

The U.S. National Human Genome Research Institute has more about genetic testing.

SOURCE: University of Washington, news release, Aug. 25, 2022

However, the GWAS database is based on populations of European ancestry, and may therefore not be representative of other populations. In this study, we investigated whether the low PRS of African populations is due to a lack of genetic signal in African genomes, or to a different relationship between PRS and disease risk in these populations.
To investigate this question, we used summary statistics from a recent GWAS meta-analysis of more than a million individuals of African ancestry, and simulated GWAS results for African populations based on previously reported LD and trait heritability estimates. We then examined whether the low PRS of African populations could be explained by low heritability estimates for complex traits, and by the structure of LD in African genomes.
We found that the low PRS of African populations cannot be explained by lower heritability or by LD structure alone. For a set of 33 complex traits, the median estimate of heritability was 0.05 for African populations, 0.10 for European populations, and 0.25 for East Asian populations. The difference in PRS between African and European individuals carried over to their simulated full-genotype data, even though the full-genome LD structure was taken from African populations, and the heritability was increased to the level of East Asians. These results suggest that the low PRS of Africans is due to the unique genetic architecture of African populations, which is not captured by the current GWAS results.
This work highlights the importance of performing GWAS in diverse populations. As most GWAS are done in individuals of European ancestry, genetic predictions of disease risk are currently inaccurate for individuals of other ancestries. Our results suggest that the genetic architecture of complex traits differ between individuals of African ancestry and other populations, and that more genetic signals for these traits in African individuals will be required to generate accurate genetic predictions for these populations. Future work should therefore aim to collect genetic data from enough diverse populations, to cover the large amount of missing genetic information for these populations.

samples.ref: በናሚቢያ የማህጸን በር ካንሰር እና ሰርቪካል ኢንትራኢፒቴሊያ ኒኦፕላዚያን ለመከላከል የቪዥዋል እና የማጣራት ግምገማ
samples.hyp:
This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) with or without cervical cytology screening compared to cervical cytology screening alone, in preventing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer in women in Namibia.

A parallel, prospective, observational study was conducted in women aged 30–69 years who attended screening at two government health facilities in Windhoek between July 2017 and March 2019. Women were either offered VIA with or without cervical cytology or cervical cytology alone. For women who had VIA, acetic acid (3%) was applied using a cotton bud on the cervical surface. Lesions were classified as atypical metaplasia (AM), low-grade or high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL or HSIL), or cancer. Cytology was performed by conventional Papanicolaou (Pap) staining. The primary outcome was the incidence of CIN and cancer diagnosed at 6-month follow-up after screening.

Among 5210 women who underwent cervical screening, 78.5% (n = 4071) were aged 30–59 years. A total of 11.8% (n = 613) of the women screened had an abnormal cytology result. Of these, 86.1% (n = 526) returned for follow-up. A total of 9.0% (n = 47) of women with cytology follow-up had CIN or cancer. Compared to cytology alone, VIA with cytology (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16–0.75, p = 0.01) and VIA without cytology (aOR 0.20, 95% CI 0.10–0.41, p = 0.0001) significantly reduced the odds of having CIN or cancer.

This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cryotherapy as a screening and treatment strategy to reduce cervical cancer related morbidity and mortality in a resource limited setting in Kisumu Nyanza province, Kenya.
A before-and-after study design was used. 
A total of 3,670 women aged 30–49 years old were recruited in the before phase. 
During the intervention, 1,933 women underwent VIA and if indicated, immediate cryotherapy. 
The primary outcome was the incidence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia of moderate or severe grade (CIN2/3) and invasive cancer, assessed among women who underwent VIA during the intervention phase, 12–23 months after VIA.
Of 1,933 women who underwent VIA, 145 (7.5%) had CIN2/3 and 3 had invasive cancer.

The objective of this study was to compare the expression of the cell cycle regulators, p53, p16, cyclin D1 and p27 in SCC of the cervix in women with and without HIV infection. Methods: A total of 123 patients with biopsy-proven SCC of the cervix were recruited from January 2008 to December 2010. Among these, 26 women were HIV seropositive. Klotho was also assessed in a subset of 20 patients. Results: The expression of p16 and p27 was significantly higher in HIV-negative patients compared to HIV-positive patients, while the expression of cyclin D1 was significantly higher in HIV-positive patients. There was no difference in the expression of p53 between the two groups. On multivariate analysis, HIV infection was the only independent predictor of p16 and p27 expression (P<0.05). The expression of p16 and p27 correlated inversely with each other. Klotho expression was decreased in HIV-positive patients when compared to HIV-negative patients (P<0.05). Conclusions: The cell cycle regulators, p16 and p27, have different expression patterns in cervical SCC in HIV-positive and HIV-negative patients, while the expression of p53 and cyclin D1 was similar in both groups.

We included adults with chronic HBV infection, treated at a tertiary referral centre in Khartoum, Sudan, between 2007 and 2017. HBV genotypes were determined, antiviral treatment history was assessed, and baseline and on-treatment laboratory parameters were reviewed. Of 1,122 patients, 106 (9.4%) were coinfected with HIV. HIV-positive patients were younger, and had a higher prevalence of being male, having a low CD4 cell count, and a high HBV viral load at presentation. Compared with HBV-monoinfected patients, those coinfected with HIV were less likely to be of genotype A (23% vs. 37%, p<0.0001) and more likely to be of genotype D (67% vs. 43%, p<0.0001). At baseline, HIV coinfected patients were more likely to have advanced fibrosis (F3/F4) on biopsy (22% vs. 10%, p<0.0001) and a higher platelet count (153 ± 75 vs. 142 ± 67 ×109/L, p = 0.02). Despite similar rates of nucleos(t)ide analog initiation, HIV coinfected patients were less likely to receive treatment for >6 months and were less likely to achieve undetectable HBV surface antigen and viral load. In a multivariable analysis, HIV coinfection was independently associated with advanced fibrosis on biopsy (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.3–4.6; p = 0.01), younger age (OR 1.1, 95% CI 1.0–1.2; p = 00.009), and lower albumin (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.97–0.99; p = 0.01). In conclusion, HBV/HIV-coinfected patients were more likely to be of advanced fibrosis on biopsy and have a higher platelet count, lower albumin, and younger age at presentation. Despite similar rates of initiation of nucleos(t)ide analogs, HIV-coinfected patients were less likely to receive treatment for >6 months and were less likely to achieve undetectable HBV surface antigen and viral load.

The Psychiatric Section of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Cape Town provided the psychiatric assessment. The frequency of psychiatric morbidity was measured using the Clinical Interview Schedule (CIS) for the World Health Organization (WHO) International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia (IPSIS). The CIS is a structured interviewing schedule based on the systematic enumeration of all psychiatric symptoms. The CIS covers the full range of psychiatric diagnoses and includes questions on social functioning, disability, and use of psychotropic medication. The CIS was administered by psychiatrists or clinical psychologists, all of whom had been trained in its use. The CIS provides an overall diagnosis as well as specific diagnoses for each of the following psychiatric disorders: schizophrenia and other psychoses, affective disorders, anxiety disorders, and somatoform disorders. Suicide risk was assessed using the Suicide Assessment Form (SAF). The SAF is a 26-item instrument that provides a quantitative estimate of suicide risk by assigning scores to items associated with suicidal behavior. The SAF has been validated in South Africa. Substance use was assessed using the Substance Use Disorder Scale (SUDDI-S). The SUDDI-S is a 26-item scale that provides a score indicative of the presence of a substance use disorder. The SUDDI-S has been validated in South African populations. Data were analyzed using STATA version 13.1.

This is one of the sites of the PREVENT trial, a randomised controlled trial investigating the effectiveness of a vaccine (known as PROVENTV or HVTN 100) to prevent infection with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS. 
The vaccine is being tested in this study because it helped protect animals against HIV-like viruses and because of the way the vaccine was made. The vaccine used in this study is not yet licensed for use in humans. It is not known if the vaccine is safe or effective for preventing HIV infection in humans. 
The goal of this study is to learn more about the safety and effectiveness of this vaccine. 
This study will enroll 5400 HIV-uninfected women between the ages of 18 and 35. Women in this study will be randomly divided into three groups. 
The first group will receive three doses of the study vaccine at Months 0, 1, and 6. 
The second group will receive three doses of a placebo (a shot of salt water). 
The third group will receive three doses of a vaccine against hepatitis A. This vaccine is not a part of the study, but it is being given to women in this group because they will be at higher risk for infection with the virus that causes hepatitis A if they engage in sexual activity. 
All of the women in the third group will also receive the study vaccine at Months 0, 2, and 6. 
The study vaccine, PROVENTV, is a live, attenuated vaccine. This means that it contains a form of the virus that is alive, but it has been weakened so it cannot cause disease. The vaccine used in this study is made from a version of the virus that causes chimpanzee immunodeficiency virus (SIV). SIV is closely related to HIV. 
The women in this study will be followed for five years. 
All of the women will be followed for two years to determine whether the vaccine has any adverse reactions (such as serious illness). 
Half of the women in each group will be followed for an additional three years to see if the vaccine is effective in preventing infection with HIV. 
Women in this study will be told if they have HIV or hepatitis A infection at the end of the study. 
The women in this study will be tested for antibodies to the virus that causes HIV. These are substances made in the body in response to infection. The women will also be tested for cell-mediated immunity to HIV, which is another way the body can respond to infection.

The results of this study show that the use of social media is associated with increased knowledge of COVID-19, healthy and unhealthy coping strategies, and mental health.  Social media use was found to be negatively associated with age, and positively associated with education level and online shopping.  Social media use was also found to be positively associated with overall knowledge about COVID-19, healthy coping strategies, and mental health.  However, social media use was not significantly associated with perceived knowledge of COVID-19, or the use of unhealthy coping strategies.  Overall, the results support previous research that has shown a positive association between social media use and health outcomes.  This study adds to the growing body of literature that is using correlation and regression analyses to better understand the role of social media use on individual’s health and mental health outcomes during the COVID-19 pandemic.  Future research should continue to use larger and more representative samples, and examine the effects of social media use on specific populations during the COVID-19 pandemic.  In addition, longitudinal research designs are recommended to understand the effects of social media use on health and mental health outcomes, and how this may change over time.  Also, research should continue to explore the mechanisms of how social media use is associated with health and mental health outcomes during a public health crisis such as the COVID-19 pandemic.  This could inform social media interventions and public health interventions, and online interventions during future public health crises.

Abstract
This study evaluates the impact of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger state, Nigeria. The study employs a qualitative research approach using a case study design. It is based on both primary and secondary data. The primary data were generated through individual semi-structured interviews with 18 women entrepreneurs operating within the study area. Observation and secondary data were generated from literature and the internet. The study revealed that insecurity in the form of banditry and kidnapping has caused a negative impact on the entrepreneurial activities of women in the study area. It further revealed that the negative impact of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities has been gendered as women bear the brunt of the effect of insecurity. The study, therefore, recommends that the Nigerian government and relevant stakeholders should do more to tackle insecurity in the study area and Niger state as a whole.

The authors note that the low level of intimate partner violence in this sample of women from the Maputo Province of Mozambique may have important implications for HIV intervention research and prevention programs. They write that "intimate partner violence may be an important factor influencing the risk of HIV transmission, as it has been shown to disrupt protective behaviors that can reduce the risk of HIV, such as condom use, and to force individuals into sexual situations that are conducive to transmission."

The researchers suggest that intervention programs that address economic empowerment of women and gender norms may be beneficial for reducing HIV risk. "Addressing gender-based inequalities and empowering women to improve their economic status and gain control over resources and decision-making may be important strategies in reducing their risk of HIV," they write.

Introduction: Selenium (Se), copper (Cu) and zinc (Zn) are essential for normal pregnancy outcome, since these trace elements are needed for normal functioning of the immune system. Se and Cu are also essential for the development of the brain and nervous system. We hypothesized that maternal serum concentrations of Se, Cu and Zn during pregnancy are associated with the risk of preterm birth (PTB).

Methods: This case-control study was conducted in eight regions in five countries in Asia and Africa: Blantyre, Malawi; Maputo, Mozambique; Umergaon and Bikaner, India; Kaski, Nepal and Mwanza, Tanzania. In total 491 PTB cases and 1175 controls were included. Cases were PTB singletons with a gestational age < 37 weeks. Controls were live born singletons delivered at ≥ 37 weeks without a known complication. Blood samples from mothers were collected and analyzed for elemental concentrations. Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were calculated using conditional logistic regression analysis, adjusted for maternal age, ethnicity, height and BMI. A total of 105 women with singleton pregnancies who delivered at ≤ 34 weeks of gestation were included in the analysis. Maternal serum concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc were measured in the second trimester of pregnancy. The odds of preterm birth were calculated by univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses. In univariable analysis, a high maternal serum concentration of selenium (≥ 103 μg/L) was associated with a 2.7-fold decreased odds of preterm birth compared to a maternal serum concentration of selenium of 50–103 μg/L (p = 0.02). No significant association was found between a high maternal serum zinc concentration (≥ 92 mg/L) and preterm birth (p = 0.9). The odds of preterm birth were increased in women with a maternal serum zinc concentration of 68–92 mg/L compared to those with a zinc concentration of 50–68 mg/L (OR 2.1 (95% CI 1.1–4.0), p = 0.04). The objective of the study was to examine the associations between preterm birth and serum concentrations of copper and zinc in maternal serum in the third trimester.
The study included 102 women with preterm delivery and 102 women with term delivery. Maternal serum concentrations of copper and zinc were measured in both groups in the third trimester of pregnancy using atomic absorption spectrometry. The median (25th-75th percentile) maternal serum concentration of copper in the third trimester of pregnancy was 65.5 (40.5-104.3) μmol/L in women with preterm delivery and 64.8 (39.8-104.0) μmol/L in women with term delivery. The median (25th-75th percentile) maternal serum concentration of zinc in the third trimester of pregnancy was 106.6 (83.6-146.3) μmol/L in women with preterm delivery and 101.2 (77.6-142.8) μmol/L in women with term delivery. In multivariate analysis, high maternal serum concentration of copper (>75th percentile) was associated with an increased risk of preterm birth (OR 2.12, 95% CI 1.08-4.17). Maternal serum concentration of zinc was not associated with the risk of preterm birth in multivariate analysis. In a subsample of women with available urine samples, the median (25th-75th percentile) urinary zinc concentration was 3.0 (2.1-4.6) mmol/24 h in women with preterm delivery and 2.8 (2.0-3.9) mmol/24 h in women with term delivery. There was no association between urinary zinc excretion and the risk of preterm birth.
In this large cohort of women with normal copper and zinc serum concentrations, a high maternal serum concentration of copper was associated with an increased risk of preterm birth. Our results suggest that copper metabolism may play a role in the etiology of preterm birth. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings.

The role of micronutrients in human health and disease is currently one of the most rapidly evolving areas in biomedical research. This is because nutrition and dietary supplements are cheap and non-invasive to test, and because they often have an important effect on health. Micronutrients with proven effects include vitamins A, B, C, D, E and K, calcium, chromium, copper, folate, iron, magnesium, manganese, phosphorus, potassium, selenium and zinc. These micronutrients are either vitamins or minerals.

The researchers, led by Karolinska Institutet’s Andreas Lundby, have previously shown that the concentration of the micronutrient zinc is much higher in plasma and brain of pregnant women who have given birth to children with a body length of 38–42 weeks of gestation, compared to women who have given birth to children with a body length of 28–36 weeks of gestation. The length of gestation is an important marker for preterm birth. The new study was designed to investigate whether zinc plays a role in the length of gestation.

The researchers conducted two parallel studies. In the first study, they measured the length of gestation in 96 women with a confirmed pregnancy, of which 47 gave birth to children with a term body length and 49 gave birth to children with a preterm body length. They also analyzed plasma and umbilical cord blood from the women. The results showed a positive correlation between zinc concentration in umbilical cord blood and the length of gestation; the higher the zinc concentration, the longer the length of gestation. The study also showed that plasma zinc concentration in the second and third trimester was lower in women who gave birth to preterm children than in women who gave birth to children with a term body length. In the second study, the researchers followed 37 pregnant women who had previously given birth to a child with a preterm body length, and measured their zinc concentration in plasma during the first, second and third trimester. The results showed that women who increased their zinc concentration during pregnancy had a longer length of gestation compared to women who did not increase their zinc concentration.

The researchers also wanted to determine if the odds of having a preterm birth were higher for women who had low amounts of one or more of the micronutrients, when compared to women who had adequate amounts of the micronutrients.

The researchers examined data from 524 women who had been part of the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) Maternal–Fetal Medicine Units (MFMU) Network of Clinical Centers. All of the women had provided blood samples, which were used to determine selenium, copper, and zinc levels. The women also had provided information about themselves, including their ethnicity and whether they smoked or drank alcohol during their pregnancies. The researchers learned whether the women had had a preterm birth by reviewing medical records.

The researchers used statistical methods to determine if the odds of having a preterm birth were higher or lower for women with high, medium, or low levels of each micronutrient, when compared with women who had adequate levels of the micronutrients. The researchers also examined whether the odds of having a preterm birth were higher for women who had low levels of more than one micronutrient, when compared with women who had adequate levels of all three micronutrients.

Our results suggest that high levels of copper and zinc are associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, and that high levels of selenium are not associated with an increased risk of preterm birth.

The researchers found that, when compared with women who had adequate levels of all three micronutrients, the odds of having a preterm birth were:

  • 2.4 times higher for women with high copper levels and adequate selenium and zinc levels
  • 2.0 times higher for women with high zinc levels and adequate copper and selenium levels
  • 1.4 times higher for women with high selenium levels and adequate copper and zinc levels

The odds of having a preterm birth were not related to medium levels of any of the micronutrients, nor were they related to low levels of copper or selenium. The odds were 1.7 times higher for women with low zinc levels than for women who had adequate zinc levels.

The researchers did not find an association between the odds of having a preterm birth and having low levels of more than one micronutrient, when compared with having adequate levels of all three micronutrients.

The women were asked about their pregnancy and delivery histories, and the researchers measured their weights and blood pressures.

The researchers tested the blood samples for antibodies to Zika virus, dengue virus, chikungunya virus, and yellow fever virus. All of the women were from areas where Zika virus is endemic, but only three of them—less than 2 percent—had ever traveled to a region where Zika virus is transmitted.

The researchers tested the blood samples for the presence of immune proteins called antibodies that are made in response to infection. If a woman had been infected with one of the four viruses before she got pregnant, the researchers could tell by looking for antibodies to those viruses in her blood sample.

But if a woman had not been infected with one of those viruses before she became pregnant, the researchers could still tell, in most cases, whether she had been infected during her pregnancy because the immune system usually makes antibodies within days to a few weeks after infection.

The researchers also tested the blood samples for the genetic material of Zika virus to see whether the women were currently infected. They tested for the genetic material of the other viruses as well, but they didn’t find any.

The researchers will follow up with the women over the next year to learn whether those who had antibodies to one or more of the viruses gave birth to babies with microcephaly or other birth defects.

Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya

The Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) is a small-bodied tortoise that is endemic to the dry areas of Kenya and Tanzania. There is little information on the ecology of this species. This study aimed to examine the homing ability and site fidelity of Pancake tortoises in their natural habitat. We conducted a series of releases of marked tortoises at sites 500 m, 1.5 km, 3 km, and 5 km away from their capture locations. We also examined the degree of territoriality of this species by counting the number of tortoises found within a 30 m radius of a marked reference tortoise.
All released tortoises homed back to their capture sites, and the percentage homed increased with the time since release (r = 0.878, d.f. = 20, P < 0.0001). The percentage homed was higher for releases closer to the capture site (mean ± SE: capture site 100%, n = 17; 500 m: 88.9% ± 5.2%, n = 28; 1.5 km: 80% ± 9.3%, n = 21; 3 km: 23.1% ± 9.9%, n = 22; 5 km: 0%, n = 11). Tortoises that did not home were found within 10 km of their release locations. The number of tortoises within 30 m of a reference tortoise was higher when the reference was released at a harem site than at a male-only site (H = 22.89, d.f. = 1, P < 0.0001).
These results show that Pancake tortoises are able to home over long distances in their natural habitat and are site faithful. Further, there is some evidence that they are territorial. The high site fidelity of this species places it at risk from threats that affect only certain locations, and suggests that habitat loss has the potential to seriously affect this species through population fragmentation.

In this study, we examined the spatial and temporal use of a novel environment by the African penguin, a species that forages in the open ocean and is known to have cognitive abilities similar to those of mammals. Feeding behavior was recorded using video and then analyzed using open-source software. The results showed that penguins exhibited a unique feeding pattern in which they alternated between feeding in the central zone and feeding in the peripheral zones. This pattern was maintained over time, with penguins returning to the central zone after feeding in the peripheral zones. The results also showed that penguins preferred to feed in the morning and in the afternoon, and that they spent more time feeding in the morning than in the afternoon. The results of this study suggest that penguins use their cognitive abilities to find and use resources in their environment. This understanding can be used to improve the welfare of penguins in captivity, and to better understand the behavior of other animals that use their environment to find resources.

Here, we study the role of religion and culture in the perception and conservation of the greater mouse-nosed bat (Rhynchostronium musculum), a threatened species endemic to the cloud forests of Costa Rica and Nicaragua. We conducted 45 semi-structured interviews with members of the Brunca and Boruca indigenous groups in southern Costa Rica, and with Costa Ricans of European descent. We used a Q-method to identify the dimensions of the subjectivity in perceptions of this species. We found significant differences in perceptions of R. musculum among the three groups. The indigenous groups had more positive perceptions of the species, associated with religious and cultural values, while the non-indigenous group had more negative perceptions associated with fear of the species and human-wildlife conflict. Among the indigenous groups, the Boruca reported the strongest attachment to the bat, which was associated with the Boruca origin myth and the belief that R. musculum provides a connection to the spirit world. The results highlight the importance of culture and religion in shaping local perceptions of species, and the need to involve local communities in conservation planning and management of threatened species.

We captured and ringed eight juvenile Pombo cansdalei in the study area in May 2016 and then tried to re-capture them in the same area in July and November of the same year. We used a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) to model recapture success as a function of month, time since capture and interaction between month and time since capture. We also used capture-recapture data to estimate the effective population size (Neff) of Pombo cansdalei in the study area. Our results showed no post-fledging site fidelity in Pombo cansdalei. This is in contrast to other pombo species that show strong site fidelity post-fledging. The lack of site fidelity might be due to the fact that the study area is a small island, and the limited amount of available habitat might force the juveniles to move to other areas in order to find a suitable habitat for breeding. The high Neff value that we estimated indicates a large number of breeding individuals in the study area. The high number of breeders might ensure the recolonization of the study area after a disturbance and thus high resilience of the population. This makes the species less vulnerable to factors that might cause a local extinction, such as habitat loss. Our results also showed that the recapture rate of Pombo cansdalei is higher in July than in November. This could be due to the fact that we could observe Pombo cansdalei in the study area until July, but none in November, which might be due to the fact that most individuals have left the area by then or that they are difficult to detect in the canopy of the forest. The study, led by the University of Bristol and the Aspinall Foundation, used satellite tracking to show that the tortoises, also known as Geochelone burchardi, can travel up to 31 miles (50km) in a single trip.

The researchers discovered that the tortoises had a unique ability to return to their home range after being translocated, as adults or as hatchlings, to a new location.

Dr Joah Hardy, postdoctoral research assistant at the University of Bristol’s School of Biological Sciences, said: “We found that these tortoises, which are listed as Endangered by the IUCN, had an impressive ability to navigate in a straight line over long distances, and an uncanny ability to find their way home, even when released hundreds of kilometres away from their birthplace.

“We believe this is the first study to demonstrate this ability in tortoises, and we hope our findings will inspire conservation efforts to protect this unique species and its habitat.”

Dr Andy Boyce, of the University of Bristol’s School of Biological Sciences, added: “We were amazed to find that the adults were able to make such long-distance journeys, but were even more surprised to find that the hatchlings displayed even better navigation skills.

“We released one group of hatchlings 25km from their birth site. They moved over 16km in two days, in the correct direction, before returning to their natal area.”

The study’s findings will be presented at a press conference at the Royal Geographic Society on Wednesday 5 December, and will be published in the journal Movement Ecology on Thursday 6 December.

The researchers from the University of Helsinki, the University of Turku, the University of Jyväskylä, the University of Antwerp, and the Royal Museum for Central Africa were surprised to see that the tortoises moved in a straight line when released far away from their home range. The animals were able to find their way back home even though they were moved over 500 meters, which is more than half the distance between the equator and either pole.

The researchers marked the home ranges of the tortoises in the Baringo National Park in Kenya with a grid of flags. They then moved the animals over 300-500 meters and marked their new location with a flag as well. After this, the animals were released in the same direction, but on the opposite side of the flag, so that they were released over 300-500 meters away from their home range. The researchers waited to see if the animals would find their way back home.

"The tortoises moved in a straight line towards the area where we had marked their home range. They walked for several hours and then stopped for the night. The next morning, they had reached their home range", explains Juha Merilä, a professor at the University of Helsinki's Faculty of Science.

The researchers repeated the experiment several times, always with the same result. The animals always moved in a straight line, even when the researchers tried to confuse them by moving the flag marking their home range.

The researchers suspect that the tortoises use the position of the Sun to find their way back home. The movement of the Sun in the sky is a reliable indicator of north when you are in the equator region. The tortoises may also use the position of the shadows to determine the direction of the north.

"The animals may also use the position of polarised light in the sky to find their way. The polarised light comes from the Sun, so the position of the polarised light also indicates the position of the Sun. The animals may use this information to find their way home", Merilä says.

“Because they are so isolated, if they get displaced, it’s really hard for them to find their way back,” said co-author Agustín Camacho, a researcher at the National University of General San Martín in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Camacho and his colleagues’ study is one of the first to investigate how animals navigate when displaced from their homes due to human activity. As climate change and urbanization continue to accelerate, more and more wildlife is being forced into contact with humans, sometimes with tragic results. But if researchers can understand how these animals navigate during such a stressful situation, they may be able to develop strategies to help protect both human interests and wildlife.

The researchers visited four tortoise populations in the province of Mendoza, Argentina, between November 2013 and March 2014. They collected location data from 41 individuals using satellite tracking devices; 10 of these individuals were tracked for more than a year. Despite the fact that the animals were displaced multiple times—likely due to harassment by farmers who considered the tortoises pests that damaged their land—the animals were able to find their way back to their home range. 

The researchers also found that the animals traveled more during the day than at night, which may be due to the fact that the tortoises were more likely to travel through agricultural areas during the day, when farmers were around to scare them off. The animals moved more than 300 meters (984 feet) in a single day. 

It’s not yet clear how the tortoises were able to find their way back to their homes, but the researchers have a few ideas. For one, the animals may have been using visual cues, such as landmarks, to guide themselves. Alternatively, they may have been using sensory cues, such as changes in temperature or the Earth’s magnetic field, to help them find their way. Further research is needed to investigate these possibilities. 

“Understanding how animals navigate during human-related displacement events may help us to develop strategies to help them avoid dangerous areas without severely restricting their movements and reducing other anthropogenic pressures,” the researchers wrote in their study.

A Prospective, Randomized, Single-Blind, Controlled Study.

R Rifampicin is a essential component of the standard treatment of tuberculous meningitis. The standard dosage is 10 mg/kg twice weekly when given orally and 10 mg/kg daily when given intravenously. However, both regimens are difficult to administer in children because of the large volume of fluid required for intravenous injection and the poor palatability of the medication when given orally. Higher doses of rifampicin given once daily have been shown to be effective and better tolerated in adults with tuberculosis, including those with tuberculosis meningitis. We hypothesized that a dose of 20 mg/kg once daily would be better tolerated and have comparable pharmacokinetics to the standard dose when given orally in children with tuberculous meningitis.
Patients and Methods
We did a prospective, randomized, single-blind, controlled study of high-dose oral versus intravenous rifampicin in children with culture-confirmed tuberculous meningitis. The study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital in Kampala, Uganda. Children were eligible for enrollment if they were between 1 month and 16 years of age and had a confirmed diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis. Exclusion criteria were prematurity, severe extra-pulmonary tuberculosis, or a terminal clinical condition. The study was approved by the institutional review boards of the Makerere University School of Medicine and the Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg School of Public Health. Written informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of each patient.
After a full explanation of the study, patients were randomized to receive either high-dose oral (20 mg/kg/once daily) or standard intravenous rifampicin (10 mg/kg/twice weekly). We examined whether lower doses of oral rifampicin could achieve serum concentrations sufficient to achieve equivalent exposure to the drug. We measured serum rifampicin concentrations in 16 children with tuberculosis receiving 10 mg/kg or 15 mg/kg of oral rifampicin and in 16 children receiving 10 mg/kg intravenous rifampicin. The area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) was 30% higher in children receiving intravenous rifampicin compared with oral rifampicin (P = 0.02). The AUC in children receiving oral rifampicin was similar to that reported in adults receiving 600 mg (10 mg/kg) of oral rifampicin (P = 0.9). Our results suggest that 600 mg of oral rifampicin produces equivalent drug exposure to 10 mg/kg intravenous rifampicin and, based on an established exposure-response relationship for rifampicin, should produce similar outcomes. Our findings support the use of 600 mg of oral rifampicin for the treatment of tuberculosis, including tuberculous meningitis, in children and adults. Simple, inexpensive, and widely available, oral rifampicin would represent a significant advance for the treatment of tuberculosis if its use is shown to be comparable with intravenous rifampicin.

Patients receiving standard antimicrobial therapy (control group) were compared with those receiving the same therapy plus the drug combination amoxicillin and clavulanate (treatment group). Plasma samples were collected up to 12 hours after the start of dosing on day 1 and at 12 and 24 hours on day 8. Amoxicillin and clavulanate concentrations were measured by high-performance liquid chromatography. The area under the concentration-time curves (AUCs) for amoxicillin and clavulanate were 24.1 versus 5.5 mg×hour/L (P<0.001) and 9.5 versus 2.7 mg×hour/L (P = 0.002), and the peak concentrations (Cmax) were 4.1 versus 1.9 mg/L (P = 0.001) and 2.6 versus 0.8 mg/L (P = 0.005), for the treatment and control groups, respectively. The AUCs for amoxicillin and clavulanate were significantly higher in the treatment group, and the Cmax for clavulanate was higher than the AUC. These data suggest that administration of amoxicillin and clavulanate is feasible in children with tuberculous meningitis and that amoxicillin is absorbed satisfactorily. The greater AUC and Cmax for clavulanate achieved with the fixed combination are likely to be clinically important in the treatment of infections caused by ampicillin-resistant organisms.

The primary endpoint was the percentage of subjects with a normalised QTc interval (ΔQTc ≤ 10 ms) and a safety margin (QTC ≤ 50 ms) 24 hours post-dose. Secondary efficacy endpoints included change in QTc from baseline and the incidence of adverse events. The safety population included all subjects who received at least one dose of tranetinib. The pharmacokinetic population included all subjects who received at least one dose of tranetinib and had at least one post-dose plasma concentration. Results: Twenty-nine patients were enrolled and received tranetinib 10 mg/kg (n = 7), 35 mg/kg (n = 15), or intravenously (n = 7). At the highest dose, the percentage of subjects with a normalised ΔQTc interval and a safety margin was 43% (95% confidence interval [CI] 25–63%) at 24 hours post-dose. The upper bound of the 95% CI for the difference in response rates between the high-dose oral group and the intravenous group exceeded the predetermined criterion of 10% (63% [95% CI 38–84%] vs. 43%, respectively). The change from baseline in QTc was larger at 24 hours post-dose for the high-dose oral group compared with the standard-dose oral group and the intravenous group. The most common adverse events were diarrhoea, nausea, and vomiting, and there were no deaths or drug-related grades 3 or 4 adverse events of cardiac origin. All pharmacokinetic parameters increased proportionally with dose, and the half-life was about 4 hours. Conclusions: Oral tranetinib at 35 mg/kg resulted in a larger change in QTc interval compared with 10 mg/kg and was generally well tolerated.

The study is the first to use a validated pharmacokinetic model to predict the efficacy of different dosing regimens in children with tuberculous meningitis. The authors say the findings have important implications for future trials of this devastating disease.
Tuberculous meningitis is a severe form of tuberculosis that affects the meninges, the protective membranes that line the brain and spinal cord. It is a life-threatening disease that predominantly affects children in low- and middle-income countries. Standard treatment for tuberculous meningitis requires a minimum of 2 months of highly toxic multidrug therapy, of which 2 months of high doses of rifampicin is a key component. However, high doses of rifampicin are not well tolerated in young children, which may reduce the effectiveness of treatment. In this study, the authors aim to determine the optimal dose and dosing regimen of rifampicin that can be administered in young children with tuberculous meningitis.
This study enrolled 20 children with culture-confirmed tuberculous meningitis. The children were randomized to receive either 10 mg/kg or 20 mg/kg of rifampicin as a single daily dose or divided doses (10 mg/kg in the morning and 10 mg/kg in the evening). The team used a validated pharmacokinetic model of rifampicin to simulate rifampicin concentrations and predict the efficacy of the different dosing regimens.
The findings show that a single daily dose of 20 mg/kg rifampicin is sufficient to achieve the target area under the concentration-time curve. The team says this dosing strategy has the potential to simplify the treatment regimen, improve adherence, and reduce treatment-related toxicity.

The simplicity of the proposed dosing regimen has the potential to improve adherence, reduce treatment-related toxicity, and ultimately improve outcomes in children with tuberculous meningitis.

The researchers tested the blood plasma of 97 patients who had recovered from tuberculosis meningitis. They looked for antibodies against rifampicin, and found that 15% of the patients who had received a standard dose of 10 mg/kg had developed antibodies, compared to 3% of those who had received a higher dose of 20 mg/kg.

"Rifampicin is one of the most important drugs for treating tuberculosis and tuberculosis meningitis," said Dr. Leen Rigouts from the ITM, who led the study. "Our results suggest that higher doses of rifampicin could improve the health of patients suffering from tuberculosis meningitis. This is important because tuberculosis meningitis is a severe form of tuberculosis that mainly affects children and has a high death rate."

The researchers believe that the antibodies against rifampicin interfere with the activity of the drug by binding to it and making it less effective. "This is a side effect of the drug that had not been studied in detail before," said Dr. Rigouts. "Our findings could help to improve the treatment of tuberculosis meningitis and other forms of tuberculosis."

Tuberculosis meningitis is a bacterial infection of the membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord. It is a serious form of tuberculosis that can cause brain damage and neurological problems. According to the World Health Organization, tuberculosis meningitis is the most common cause of death from tuberculosis in children worldwide.

The researchers plan to further investigate the relationship between antibodies against rifampicin and the activity of the drug. They also plan to test the blood plasma of patients who are currently suffering from tuberculosis meningitis to see if they have developed antibodies against rifampicin.

In addition to Dr. Rigouts, the study was conducted by a team of researchers from the ITM, the University of Antwerp, and the Rifinix study group. The study was funded by the Research Foundation - Flanders (FWO) and the Belgian government.

The researchers believe that the higher doses were more effective because they maintained higher blood plasma levels of rifampicin, the main ingredient in the drug.

This is an example of how big clinical trials can miss important effects. The researchers of this trial had to stop the trial early because it was conducted as a so-called non-inferiority trial. Such a trial is conducted to prove that a new drug or a new treatment is not worse (i.e. inferior) than the old one. In this case the researchers wanted to prove that the higher doses were not worse than the standard dose, which they in fact succeeded to do. However, this trial was not designed to show that the higher doses were better than the standard dose.

If the researchers of this trial had wanted to show that the higher doses were better than the standard dose, they would have had to design their study as a so-called superiority trial, and they would have had to include many more patients — at least several thousands — and the study would have had to last several years. Since the resources for conducting clinical trials are limited, such superiority trials are rarely conducted.

Conducting a superiority trial is a difficult challenge, and it is important that such trials are conducted when there is a clear expectation that the new treatment is likely to be better than the old one. When we want to study if a new treatment is better than an old one, the chances are high that the new treatment will turn out to be at most equivalent to the old one — because of, for instance, the placebo effect, the natural course of the disease or the natural regenerative capacity of the body. If there is no clear expectation that the new treatment is likely to be better, it is not worth the effort conducting a costly superiority trial that will most likely not show that the new treatment is better.

The ideal situation is that we can use so-called indirect treatment comparisons. By using so-called network meta-analysis we can use the results of multiple non-inferiority trials to indirectly compare different treatments.

A laboratory incubation study

The effects of combined compost and biochar application on soil quality were evaluated in a laboratory incubation study performed on a highly weathered coastal savanna soil (Aerenosols). Compost (5% w/w) and biochar (5% w/w) were added to the soil, either as individual treatments or in combination, and the resulting incubated soil samples were stored at 25 °C and 60% field capacity for 0, 2, 4, 8, and 16 weeks. Combined application of compost and biochar resulted in higher soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks compared to compost or biochar alone after 4 and 8 weeks of incubation, and the combined treatment performed the best in terms of basal respiration, microbial biomass, soil respiration, and potential mineralizable carbon (PMC), with increases of 122, 76, 33, and 47 mg CO2/g soil, respectively, after 2 weeks of incubation. The compost and biochar amendments also resulted in increased basal respiration and microbial biomass C after 2 weeks of incubation, although these increases were higher for compost than biochar. After 2 weeks of incubation, the highest microbial biomass C was measured for the combined compost and biochar treatment, followed by compost alone, then biochar alone. The compost and biochar amendments led to increased soil respiration after 2 weeks of incubation, and the combined treatment resulted in the highest increase in soil respiration (33 mg CO2/g soil), followed by biochar alone (30 mg CO2/g soil), and then compost alone (23 mg CO2/g soil). The highest PMC was observed for the combined compost and biochar treatment (478.5 mg CO2/g soil), followed by compost alone (470.2 mg CO2/g soil), and then biochar alone (438.0 mg CO2/g soil). The results suggest that the combined compost and biochar application can improve the quality of a highly weathered coastal savanna soil.

samples.hyp:
The most widespread and economic soil fertility management option is the application of mineral fertilizers. However, the use of fertilizers in sub-Saharan Africa is of limited extent. While the main reason for the low fertilizer use intensity is the limited purchasing power of the small-scale farmers, lack of information on the need for fertilizers and on their efficient and effective use, and limited access to credit are additional factors of importance.

The overall objective of this project is to improve the information base for increased and efficient use of fertilizers in smallholder farming systems in sub-Saharan Africa, with the ultimate goal of increasing production, food security, and farmers’ incomes.

The specific objectives of the project are to:

1. Improve the information base for fertilizer use in smallholder farming systems in sub-Saharan Africa.

2. Improve understanding of farmers’ fertilizer decision-making processes.

3. Analyze factors constraining effective and efficient fertilizer use.

4. Develop and adapt decision aids to assist smallholder farmers in adopting more efficient ways of using fertilizers.

5. Improve recommendations on fertilizer use.

6. Develop and adapt a training manual for extension workers.

The overall impact of the project is to contribute to the improved use of fertilizers in smallholder farming systems in sub-Saharan Africa.

The direct beneficiaries of the research results are extension services. Indirect beneficiaries are smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa.

The research results will be disseminated to the target group of smallholder farmers through training of extension workers.

The research results will also be disseminated through normal publications in journals and at national and international meetings and conferences.

The research will be carried out in project sites in Kenya, Tanzania, and Ethiopia. The countries were selected on the basis of existing collaboration between participants and partners in these countries and the need for projects on fertilizers in the countries.

The project will be carried out in collaboration with the Kenya, Tanzania, and Ethiopia partners. The partners from the respective countries are involved in the planning and implementation of the project through the project steering committees at country level. The partners will also be involved in the data collection and in providing the study sites. The project will also be carried out in collaboration with the International Fertilizer Industry Association (IFA) and the International Fertilizer Development Center (IFDC).

Therefore, the main objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of biochar and compost, either alone or in combination, on soil properties and Bradyrhizobium spp. population and activity. We also aimed to identify the biochar dose and compost rate that give the best results in terms of soil quality and biological N2 fixation. However, the combined application of biochar and compost improved the soil properties better than the individual applications. The highest N2 fixation (148 kg Nha−1 yr−1) was also obtained when the soil was amended with 15 mg N g−1 of biochar and 100% compost. The incubation experiment was done in a completely randomized design with three replicates for each treatment. The pH, electrical conductivity (EC), organic carbon (OC), nitrate (NO3−) and available phosphorus (P) were determined for each treatment at 0, 10, 20 and 30 days after incubation. The results showed that the amendment of acrisol with biochar or compost increased the pH and available P, and decreased EC and DOC. The amendment of acrisol with biochar at a rate of 1 % increased the OC at 30 days after incubation. The amendment of acrisol with cbio and rbio increased NO3− at 30 days after incubation. The amendment of acrisol with compost, cbio, rbio and cocomp increased the available P at 30 days after incubation. The amendment of acrisol with compost, cbio, rbio, coco700, cocomp and rcocomp increased the OC at 30 days after incubation. The amendment of acrisol with compost, cbio, rbio, cocomp and rcocomp decreased EC at 30 days after incubation. The highest available P and OC contents at 30 days after incubation were observed in the treatments with compost, cbio, rbio, cocomp and rcocomp. The highest NO3− content at 30 days after incubation was observed in the treatments with cbio and rbio. The lowest EC content at 30 days after incubation was observed in the treatments with compost, cbio, rbio, cocomp, rcocomp and coco700. The results from this study suggest that the amendment of acrisol with biochar or compost can improve its quality by increasing the available P and OC contents and decreasing the EC content.

samples.hyp: The experiment was conducted in the greenhouse of the University of California, Berkeley, USA. The experiment followed a completely randomized design with three replications. The treatments were applied to soil in 1.5 m long by 0.9 m wide by 0.3 m high plastic beds. The treatments were applied to the soil surface and raked into the top 5 cm of the soil. The beds were planted with broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis) in 30 cm rows with 20 cm between plants. The plants were watered daily and weeded as needed. The experiment was harvested 84 days after transplanting. Three soil cores (2 cm diameter and 7.5 cm deep) were randomly collected from each plot at harvest using a soil corer. Soil cores were kept at 4 °C until analysis. Soil respiration was measured in the field using a LI-6400 system (LI-COR, Lincoln, NE, USA) with an infrared gas analyzer. The system was equipped with a static chamber with clear acrylic top and sides and a soil collar positioned at a soil depth of 7.5 cm. The chamber was installed in the field and left for 2 weeks before the first measurement to allow the soil to acclimate to the chamber. Three measurements of soil respiration were taken at 0, 30 and 60 min after installing the chamber. The measurements were taken at the same time of day to minimize the effect of light intensity on soil respiration. The maximum value obtained during the 60 min was used to represent basal soil respiration. Soil samples for the determination of microbial carbon, available nitrogen, and pH were collected in 15 mL centrifuge tubes. The samples were kept at 4 °C and analyzed within 14 days. Soil pH was analyzed using a pH meter (Orion Star 15, Thermo Scientific, MA, USA). The available nitrogen in the soil was extracted using 1 M KCl and analyzed using the Branauer–Totutis–Kjeldahl method (KjELtec 2300, Foss, Hillerød, Denmark) . Soil microbial carbon was measured as the total organic carbon minus the inorganic carbon, which was determined by the loss of weight after heating the sample at 360 °C for 24 h . Biochar alone increased available water holding capacity by 0.8 kg/kg, exchangeable Ca by 1.04 cmolc/kg, and available P by 16.2 mg/kg, although the differences were not significant. The combined application of biochar and compost increased available water holding capacity by 1.05 kg/kg, exchangeable K by 0.44 cmolc/kg, exchangeable Ca by 1.23 cmolc/kg, and available P by 21.1 mg/kg in comparison to the un-amended control. The highest available P was observed in the soil treated with composted biochar, and the highest exchangeable Ca and K in the soil treated with a combination of biochar and compost. The highest microbial biomass was also found in the soil treated with composted biochar, and the highest basal respiration in the soil treated with biochar and compost. The application of biochar and compost, either solely or combined, improved soil quality in terms of increased available water holding capacity, exchangeable Ca, K, and available P, as well as increased microbial biomass and basal respiration. The increase in available P and exchangeable Ca was most pronounced when biochar was composted prior to soil amendment.

Palestinian farmers in the West Bank have long struggled to grow healthy crops due to poor soil quality. Now, thanks to a new USAID-funded project, the Palestinian Agricultural Research Center (PARC) is testing the use of biochar and compost to improve soil health. The project, which is part of the Middle Eastern and North Africa (MENA) Vegetable Improvement Network (VIN), is led by PARC and includes research partners from the University of Delaware, the University of Georgia, and the International Center for Biosaline Agriculture in Dubai.

Biochar is a type of charcoal that is produced from plant material and is known for its ability to sequester carbon while providing various nutrients to plants. Compost, on the other hand, is a natural fertilizer made from organic matter that can improve soil structure, increase water holding capacity, and supply essential nutrients to plants.

In a recent field trial, the research team tested biochar and compost application rates on different soil types. The team found that a combination of biochar and compost significantly improved soil quality, especially for heavy clay soils. The addition of biochar and compost increased soil organic matter, improved soil structure, and increased the availability of nutrients like phosphorus and sulfur.

The biochar produced at 700 °C was used as a soil amendment in a greenhouse experiment to determine its effect on nutrient retention and plant growth. The researchers added 25 tons/ha of the 700 °C biochar to the soil. They grew maize (Zea mays) and cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) in the soil with and without the addition of biochar. The researchers found that the addition of biochar increased the retention of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and calcium (Ca) in the soil. The maximum amount of N, P, K, and Ca retained in the soil was 43.2%, 17.6%, 22.8%, and 41.1% respectively of the amount added with biochar. The addition of biochar also increased the height, number of leaves, and shoot and root dry biomass of the maize and cowpea plants. The maximum increase in height was 35.2% for the maize plants and 31.4% for the cowpea plants; the maximum increase in the number of leaves was 31.1% for the maize plants and 32.2% for the cowpea plants; and the maximum increase in shoot and root dry biomass was 59.2% for the maize plants and 56.8% for the cowpea plants. The researchers concluded that the coconut husk biochar produced at 700 °C can be used as a soil amendment to increase nutrient retention and plant growth.

The biochars were added to soil at rates of 20, 40, and 60 Mg ha−1 and mixed thoroughly into the top 20 cm of soil. The same rates of a nonorganic carbon (OC), glucose, and sucrose were also added as a reference. Soil samples were collected before and after the amendment and analyzed for OC and microbial biomass carbon (MB-C) using a variety of methods. The results showed that the addition of biochar to soil increased both soil OC and MB-C. The increase in OC was persistent in the top 50 cm of soil 12 months after the amendment. The increase in MB-C was greater with the addition of biochar produced at lower temperatures, and MB-C normalized to soil organic carbon (SOC) was greater with the addition of biochar produced at higher temperatures. The microbial biomass ratio (MB-C/SOC) increased with the addition of biochar produced at all temperatures. The addition of glucose and sucrose increased MB-C in the top 10 cm of soil; however, the increase in MB-C normalized to SOC was only significant with the addition of sucrose. The results also showed that the increase in MB-C and the microbial biomass ratio was greater with the addition of biochar than a comparable amount of glucose or sucrose.

The study, published today in Nature Sustainability, shows that applying biochar to soil can increase crop yields and reduce the need for inorganic fertilizers, thereby improving the quality and sustainability of the soil while also saving costs for farmers.

The international team of researchers, including the University of Sheffield and the Swiss Federal Research Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research (WSL), used a suite of modelling approaches to simulate the long-term effects of different farming practices on soil quality and crop yields in sub-Saharan Africa.

The researchers applied their models to four different sites in the region, and found that adding biochar to soil significantly increased crop yields, improved soil quality and reduced the need for inorganic fertilizer.

The researchers also showed that the effects of biochar on soil and crop yield were greater when combined with other measures, such as adding rock minerals to the soil or growing cowpea - a type of legume - as a preceding crop.

Dr. Simone Pascucci, from the University of Sheffield's Grantham Centre for Sustainable Futures, said: "Our analysis shows that biochar has the potential to improve the quality and sustainability of soils, while at the same time increasing crop yields and reducing the need for inorganic fertilizers in sub-Saharan Africa.

Co-author Dr. Philippe Ciais, from the Laboratory for Earth System Research at the French National Institute for Sustainable Development and the Laboratory for Geochemistry at the French National Centre for Scientific Research, said: "We found that the use of biochar can bring substantial benefits to both the environment and farmers' profits in sub-Saharan Africa.

Lead author Dr. Matthias Kirschke, from the WSL, said: "Our results suggest that biochar can help to improve the quality of soils, but further research is needed to confirm the findings and to thoroughly assess the costs and benefits of the different farming practices."

Prof. Julia Meyer, from the University of Sheffield's Grantham Centre for Sustainable Futures, added: "Soil is a finite resource that is essential for food production, and its sustainability must be maintained to secure future global food supplies.

The study was funded by the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program.
