The first part of my thesis deals with the influence of the genetic variant R501X on the structure of the fibrin fibre network in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). This variant results in the replacement of a single amino acid, Arginine for Glycine at position 501 in the fibrinogen molecule. The replacement of glycine by such a large side chain as the charged arginine is likely to have a dramatic effect on the fibrin polymerase activity, conformation and stability. In the first publication based on this thesis, we have shown for the first time that the R501X variant results in a decreased number of long and thick fibres and an increased number of short thin fibres compared to tissues without this variant. This altered fibre structure could be an explanation for the increased susceptibility for thrombosis in RA, as it has been suggested that the thick fibres are more likely to undergo lysis than the thin fibres. However, both fibrin fibre types were found to be associated with the deposition of immunoglobulin G (IgG) and the activation of the alternative complement pathway, suggesting that the local immune response is more important for the increased thrombosis risk than the fibrin fibre structure per se. This part of the thesis has been published in several scientific journals.

The second part of this thesis deals with the cellular immune response in RA, more specifically the role of CD4+CD438R+ T-cells in the pathogenesis of RA. This T-cell subset has been suggested to be involved in the inflammatory process, probably through the secretion of cytokines and chemokines. In the second publication based on this thesis, we have shown that the percentage of CD4+CD438R+ T-cells is higher in RA patients compared to healthy controls, and that these cells are activated as measured by the expression of CD69. We have also shown that the CD4+CD438R+ T-cells are involved in the immune response to autologous fibrin, as they are attracted to fibrin fibrils in vitro, and express molecules involved in the removal of apoptotic cells. These cells may, together with other immune cells, be involved in the removal of apoptotic synovial fibroblasts, which probably play a key role in the pathology of RA. This part of the thesis has been published in a scientific journal.

We hypothesized that fibrin formed in the presence of citrullinated fibrin(ogen) would exhibit altered biophysical properties and enhanced thrombogenicity. Recombinant, citrullinated and noncitrullinated human fibrin(ogen), and fibrin formed from both isotypes were investigated by electrospray ionization mass spectrometry, electron microscopy, turbidity, thromboelastography, and thrombus formation in vivo. Citrullination resulted in conformational changes in both fibrin(ogen) isoforms. Fibrin formed from citrullinated fibrin(ogen) was more transparent than controls, had a more open matrix, decreased fiber stiffness, and increased water content. Thromboelastography and in vivo data demonstrated that citrullination strongly enhanced the thrombogenicity of both fibrin(ogen) isotypes. These findings provide a mechanistic link between autoimmunity, citrullination, and altered fibrin(ogen) function that may contribute to accelerated atherothrombosis in rheumatoid arthritis.
Source: Journal of thrombosis and thrombolysis, 2018; 45 (1) pp 88-97

We hypothesized that vascular dysfunction, inflammation and coagulation are linked and that these links may be perturbed in RA. We further hypothesized that this perturbation is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular events. Our results show that measures of vascular function and inflammation are related, that fibrin clot structure is different in patients with RA and that RA patients have an altered interaction between vascular function, inflammation and coagulation. We also provide the first description of enhanced expression of tissue factor in monocytes of RA patients. This study provides new insights into the dysregulation of the vascular, inflammatory and coagulation systems in RA and supports the concept that these systems are interconnected and are all affected in RA. Our results, however, also suggest that each of these systems shows specific alterations in RA patients. Future studies aiming at identification of novel biomarkers or identification of patients at risk should therefore not only focus on measurements of vascular function, inflammation or coagulation alone but take measurements of all three into account.

The TEG thrombin-clotting assay is a simple, rapid, and sensitive method to measure the in vitro coagulation status and to assess global hemostasis and/or anticoagulant effect of drugs or disease state. The TEG parameters are closely correlated with the corresponding clinical data. A number of studies have been published using TEG in various clinical fields such as heart surgery, liver disease, and hematology. The TEG has been shown to be a useful method to monitor the hemostatic function during liver transplantation, to assess the bleeding risk in patients with liver cirrhosis, and to identify patients with a high risk of blood loss during cardiac surgery. Ex vivo thrombus formation under flow conditions as assessed by the TEG has been shown to correlate with in vivo thrombosis in a rabbit model. The TEG has also been used to measure the effect of various drugs on coagulation and fibrinolysis. For example, TEG has been used to investigate the effect of different anticoagulants (heparin, aprotinin, and protamine) and antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel, and enoxaparin) on coagulation.

In patients with RA, the prothrombin time is normal, whereas the partial thromboplastin time and the thrombin time are increased. The increase in the partial thromboplastin time is the most consistent finding and may be the only laboratory parameter that differentiates patients with active RA from patients with inactive RA or other inflammatory conditions. The increased thrombin time and the increased partial thromboplastin time result from the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies that are found in a large percentage of patients with RA. These antibodies interfere with the activation of clotting factors and also with the generation of thrombin. The presence of these antibodies in patients with RA may be important because patients with RA who have these antibodies have been found to be at increased risk of thromboembolic complications.

The study was carried out by researchers from the University of Bristol, in collaboration with colleagues from the Arthritis Research UK Centre for Excellence in Epidemiology at the University of Manchester.

The findings suggest that understanding the link between rheumatoid arthritis and cardiovascular disease could be key to improving patient outcomes.

The study, published in the Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases, analysed data from over 46,000 individuals, aged 39-69 years, from 14 European countries. A total of 1,616 incident cases of rheumatoid arthritis were identified and 2,802 cases of first ever myocardial infarction (heart attack).

The results showed that rheumatoid arthritis was associated with a 51% higher risk of myocardial infarction before diagnosis, and a 71% higher risk after diagnosis.

The authors believe their results provide a basis for further research to identify the underlying mechanisms that link the two conditions.

Dr Emanuela Orini, lead author and Research Fellow at the University of Bristol’s Centre for Causal Inference and Translational Epidemiology, said: “Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of mortality in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, but the mechanisms driving this increased risk are not fully understood. Importantly, there is evidence to suggest that cardiovascular disease can be under-recognised in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Our findings suggest that it may be important to identify these patients early and offer support to reduce their risk.”

Professor Rebecca Richmond, co-author and Programme Leader for Epidemiology at the Arthritis Research UK Centre for Excellence in Epidemiology at the University of Manchester, said: “Rheumatoid arthritis and cardiovascular disease are common chronic conditions that share several risk factors, such as smoking, poor diet and obesity. These factors contribute to an increased risk of both conditions. However, it is important to understand whether specific links exist between rheumatoid arthritis and cardiovascular disease that are not explained by these shared risk factors. This research uses novel methods to investigate whether there is a link between rheumatoid arthritis and the risk of a first heart attack. While the authors cannot prove a causal relationship due to the observational nature of the data, these results add to the body of evidence that this may be the case. More research is needed to confirm this association and to understand how to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease in this group of patients with rheumatoid arthritis.”

samples.hyp: When a blood vessel is damaged, a complex set of chemical reactions kick in, triggering a cascade of events that can lead to dangerous blood clots. One of the first reactions is the activation of blood platelets, small fragments of cells that line the walls of blood vessels. Activated platelets release chemicals that attract more platelets to the injury site, and also signal the body to form a blood clot. This clot, or thrombus, is a solid mass of blood cells and fibrin—-a protein involved in blood clotting. It forms outside the blood vessel at the site of injury, and then moves inside the vessel to plug the hole. This process, known as hemostasis, is essential for stopping bleeding, but it can also block the normal flow of blood through a blood vessel. Inflammation can disrupt this process by altering the way platelets and fibrin function. For example, research shows that inflammation can activate platelets even in the absence of injury, leading to the formation of blood clots outside the blood vessel. This is known as a thrombus or deep vein thrombosis (DVT). DVT can be particularly dangerous because it occurs in deep veins where it may go undetected, and can break loose, travel through the bloodstream, and block an artery in the lungs or elsewhere (a pulmonary embolism). Inflammation can also increase the amount of fibrin produced during the blood clotting process, leading to the formation of a large, potentially dangerous clot. In addition, inflammation can lead to the degradation of nitric oxide, a chemical that helps keep blood vessels healthy and blood flowing properly. The result is reduced blood flow, which can make it more likely for a blood clot to form. Finally, inflammation can alter the activity of an enzyme called tissue plasminogen activator, or tPA. This enzyme is essential for dissolving blood clots, but during inflammation its activity is decreased, meaning that blood clots are more likely to form and persist. Taken together, these effects increase the risk of dangerous blood clots, particularly in individuals with existing risk factors such as age, family history, or other health conditions. It is important to note that inflammation does not always lead to blood clots, and many other factors are involved in the blood clotting process. However, understanding the link between inflammation and blood clotting is crucial for developing strategies to prevent and manage blood clots in individuals at risk. They found that RA patients who had a history of smoking were at the greatest risk of CVD, and that RA patients who had never smoked were not at an increased risk of CVD. This indicates that RA is an independent risk factor for CVD, and that smoking is the key factor that increases the risk of CVD in RA patients. The researchers suggest that smoking-related inflammation may be one of the mechanisms by which smoking increases the risk of CVD in RA patients.

The researchers also found that RA patients who had a history of smoking were at increased risk of all-cause mortality, independent of CVD. This indicates that smoking is an independent risk factor for mortality in RA patients.

The researchers used data from the Norwegian RA register and the Norwegian CardioVascular Register, which included 55,932 RA patients. They linked these data with data from the Norwegian Cancer Registry and the National Population Register to investigate the risk of CVD, CVD mortality, and all-cause mortality in RA patients.

During a median follow-up period of 8.2 years, 1,721 RA patients were diagnosed with CVD. The researchers adjusted their analyses to account for various factors that might influence the risk of CVD, including age, sex, smoking status, socioeconomic status, and treatment with statins or anti-coagulant therapy. Even after adjusting for these factors, the researchers found that RA patients who had a history of smoking had a 56% increased risk of CVD compared with RA patients who had never smoked.

The researchers also found that RA patients who had a history of smoking had a 3.2-fold increased risk of all-cause mortality compared with RA patients who had never smoked. This increased risk of mortality was independent of the risk of CVD.

The researchers concluded that smoking is the key factor that increases the risk of CVD and all-cause mortality in RA patients. They suggest that RA treatment strategies that aim to reduce the risk of CVD should specifically target RA patients who smoke.

They found that the fibrin clots formed much faster in the RA group than in the healthy people.

samples.ref: የባህር ላይ ሜትሮሎጂ ትንበያዎች ለባህር ዳርቻ ውቅያኖስ ተጠቃሚዎች - አመለካከቶች ፣ አጠቃቀም እና አወሳሰድ
samples.hyp:
B. Alvesa, M. S. Schepens, A. C. Bricchetti, A. C. da Silva, M. A. B. Garcia, E. C. Barbioli, and A. M. B. Rocha
Atmos. Sci. Lett., 2023; 24 (1) 100325
DOI: 10.1016/j.asle.2022.100325
The use of marine meteorological information by coastal ocean users may improve the safety and efficiency of marine operations. This study analyzed the perceptions, usability, and uptake of marine meteorological forecasts by coastal ocean users. Data were collected through an online questionnaire survey and semi-structured interviews with 17 coastal ocean users in Brazil. Results from the questionnaire were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and those from the interviews using an inductive approach. Coastal ocean users perceived that marine meteorological information is relevant, but they are not using it due to difficulties in accessing and interpreting the information. The main challenges to access forecasts were identified as low user confidence in online forecast platforms and a lack of training in marine meteorology. The format of the marine forecasts was considered by coastal ocean users as a hindrance to its use, as it is too complex for them to interpret. This study highlights the importance of communication and training to improve the use of marine meteorological forecasts by coastal ocean users.

The usability gap refers to the difference between the amount of scientific information that is available to the public and the amount of information that the public understands and finds useful. The usability gap has been identified as a significant barrier to effective science communication. In this study, we examined the perceived usability of scientific information among the general public (N = 765) in the United States. We found that the public has a general understanding of the concepts of basic science, such as what a hypothesis is and the scientific method, but has a more limited understanding of scientific findings specific to a discipline, such as physics or biology. We also examined the association between participants’ perceptions of the usability of scientific information and their attitudes and behaviors related to science communication. Our findings suggest that the public is interested in receiving scientific information and would like to participate in discussions about science, but they feel that they do not have the scientific knowledge or language to fully participate in these discussions. There is a need for researchers to develop effective ways of communicating complex scientific information to the public. This is especially important in the context of the current COVID-19 pandemic, where scientific information is critical for people to protect themselves and others from infection. Our findings also suggest that efforts to promote public understanding of science should focus on the general concepts of science and not solely on the details of specific scientific findings. This could include highlighting the ways that science affects people’s daily lives, the values and ethics that guide scientific research, or the applications of scientific findings in real-world contexts. Additionally, it is important to provide opportunities for the public to engage in discussions and deliberations about scientific issues, such as through community forums or online platforms. This could allow individuals to ask questions, share perspectives, and learn from experts and each other. Overall, our findings emphasize the importance of bridging the usability gap to effectively communicate scientific information to the public and promote public understanding of science. This can help people make informed decisions based on the best available scientific evidence and engage in meaningful ways with the scientific enterprise.

The aim of this research is to develop a better understanding of the importance of metocean information to coastal users and to identify the information that is most relevant to their decision-making. This information will be used to develop a coastal information system that will support more informed decisions in the future. The system will integrate metocean and ecological information to provide a more holistic view of coastal hazards and support better informed decisions for sustainable use of coastal resources. The system will be developed using a human-centered design approach that is underpinned by a sound understanding of the context in which it will be used. In this research, the context includes users’ perceptions of the environment in which they make decisions, the importance and source of information on which they rely, and the processes they use to make decisions. To understand this context, a series of semi-structured interviews will be conducted with users in each country. The interviews will explore users’ perceptions of weather and ocean information and how they use this information in their day-to-day activities and decision-making processes. The interviews will also investigate the events that users find most challenging and the information that would be most helpful to them in such situations. The research will focus on four different user groups in each country: commercial fishermen, recreational fishermen, coastal tourism operators, and coastal managers. The interviews will be conducted in each of the two countries in English and locally appropriate languages. The interview data will be analyzed using a thematic analysis approach to identify common themes and perceptions across the user groups and countries. The outcomes of this research will be presented to users and other key stakeholders for input into the development of the coastal information system. The information system will be developed in consultation with these stakeholders. The research outcomes will also be presented at professional conferences and in journal articles.

The first research question was: How do farmers in the Western Cape make decisions about when to apply herbicides? The second research question was: How do farmers in the Western Cape make decisions about which herbicide to use? The third research question was: How do farmers in the Western Cape make decisions about the rate of herbicide to apply?

The survey was distributed to 1 000 randomly selected Western Cape commercial grain farmers. A total of 142 farmers returned the questionnaire, resulting in a response rate of 14.2%. The majority of the farmers who returned the questionnaire were male (96.5%), white (85.9%) and English-speaking (86.6%). The average age of the farmers was 50.6 years, and the average farm size was 1 558 hectares.

The majority of the farmers indicated that they make decisions about when to apply herbicides based on the growth stage of the crop (84.5%). The second most common response was to apply herbicides when the crop reaches a certain height (15.2%). Very few farmers indicated that they base their decisions on rainfall (2.8%) or the start of the planting season (1.4%). The majority of the farmers (82.8%) apply a pre-emergence herbicide, 14.1% of the farmers apply a post-emergence herbicide and 3.5% of the farmers apply both a pre- and post-emergence herbicide. The most commonly applied herbicide is either Atrazine or Glyphosate. The majority of farmers (87.7%) apply the recommended rate, 6.3% of the farmers apply a lower rate and 5.6% of the farmers apply a higher rate.

The majority of the farmers indicated that they make decisions about the rate of herbicide to apply based on the expected weed infestation (88.7%). The second most common response was to apply the herbicide according to the manufacturer’s instructions (10.4%). Very few farmers indicated that they base their decisions on the cost of the herbicide (0.7%) or the cost of application (0.7%). The majority of the farmers (80.3%) apply the herbicide at a rate of 0.5 to 1 litre per hectare, 7.7% of the farmers apply a rate lower than 0.5 litres per hectare and 7.7% of the farmers apply a rate higher than 1 litre per hectare.

Respondents were asked to rate their agreement with the statement "I use the Internet to access social networking sites" on a 5-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 3 = neither agree nor disagree, 5 = strongly agree). In addition, participants were asked to indicate the number of hours they used the Internet in the previous week. The following questions were used to assess participants' attitudes towards the Internet: "I feel that the Internet is a useful tool for my life" and "I feel that the Internet has a negative impact on my life". These items were adopted from previous studies (Ko, 2005; Tsai & Jang, 2009) and were rated on a 5-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 3 = neither agree nor disagree, 5 = strongly agree). To assess participants' Internet addiction, we used a Chinese version of the Internet Addiction Test (IAT; Tian et al., 2010). The IAT consists of 18 items, 9 of which are related to problems caused by excessive Internet use and 9 of which are related to positive effects of Internet use. Each item was rated on a 5-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 3 = neither agree nor disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Reliability analysis of the Chinese version of the IAT indicated a satisfactory internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .83). The Chinese version of the IAT has been shown to have good convergent and discriminant validities (Tian et al., 2010). Finally, we used the Chinese version of the Big Five Personality Test (FFPI; Xiao, 2003) to assess participants' personality. The FFPI is a 30-item questionnaire that includes the five factors of neuroticism, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness to experience. Each item was rated on a 5-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 3 = neither agree nor disagree, 5 = strongly agree). The FFPI has been shown to have good reliability and validity (Xiao, 2003; Xia et al., 2006). Table 1 provides a summary of the questionnaires used in the present study.

The research team developed a decision-making framework that describes the interrelationships among groups of people, information, and the environment. The framework was used to identify key decision-making situations that may influence information needs. The research team also developed a decision-making culture model that describes how different groups may value and use information in the context of a decision. The model was used to identify four unique decision-making cultures that may influence information needs of coastal ocean users. The four decision-making cultures are: (1) Science-based, (2) Collaborative, (3) Top-down, and (4) Bottom-up. A science-based decision-making culture values scientific information and places a high priority on gathering and producing scientific information. A collaborative decision-making culture values scientific and local (i.e., lay) information equally and places a high priority on consensus building. A top-down decision-making culture values scientific information and places a high priority on gathering and producing scientific information. A bottom-up decision-making culture values local (i.e., lay) information and places a high priority on consensus building. The decision-making culture model was used to conduct a series of semi-structured interviews with individuals involved in coastal ocean management. The interviews were conducted in California, Florida, and Oregon. A total of 60 individuals were interviewed, including commercial and recreational fishermen, aquaculturists, coastal engineers, coastal scientists, natural resource managers, and representatives from non-governmental organizations. The interviews were recorded and transcribed. The interview transcripts and the decision-making framework were used to identify situations that may influence the information needs of coastal ocean users. The information obtained through this research will help coastal ocean users, information managers, and scientists better understand the nature of the information they need to make decisions and how this information is used by various groups of coastal ocean users. This, in turn, will assist coastal ocean users and information managers in determining what information should be collected and developed to support their decisions.

The method is designed to test this assumption by examining the extent to which individuals within a group share a common set of perceptions about a particular topic. Dr. Suominen said, “Our results suggest that the forecasts may be more useful for organisations that can use the information in a different way, for instance to plan the number of staff required at different times. But we think there is room for improving the forecasts so that they are more useful for individuals as well.” The researchers now hope to work with weather forecasting organisations to see whether they can use their data to improve the accuracy of forecasts for the general public. Co-author Professor James Currie, from the University of Otago, said, “We’d like to think that our research could eventually lead to better forecasts for all New Zealanders. Elke Greifeneder, Marc Moonen, Estrella Ortega, and Norbert Neumair (2014). Weather Forecasting: The Role of Prediction Accuracy and Service Quality for User Satisfaction and Behaviour. Psychologische Beiträge, 56: 364-377. doi: 10.1027/2151-2604/a000228.
Abstract:
People frequently use weather forecasts to plan their daily activities. The main purpose of this diary study was to investigate factors that influence an individual's weather forecasting behaviour. Thirty-one weather forecast users kept a diary over a period of four weeks, in which they noted every time they used a weather forecasting service. In addition, they indicated their satisfaction with the service they used and the quality of the information they considered important for their everyday life. Results showed that prediction accuracy had a positive effect on user satisfaction, but not on the number of weather forecasts checked. Service quality, in contrast, positively affected both variables. Moreover, users were more satisfied with and more likely to use the weather forecasting service if they had used it before. The findings are discussed with regard to the theory of goal-directed behavior and the technology acceptance model.

samples.ref: የግብርና የአየር ንብረት-ብልህነት እርምጃዎች ግምገማ አሳታፊ አቀራረብ፤
samples.hyp:
A Case Study in Northern Benin

English:
The need to intervene in the agricultural sector to improve its performance and ensure food security is increasingly acknowledged. Yet, given the diverse and often conflicting goals and values of the different stakeholders involved, it is not straightforward to identify the most suitable intervention. In this context, the concept of climate-smart agriculture (CSA) has emerged as a useful framework to guide intervention planning and help ensure that they contribute to achieving co-benefits for food security, resilience to climate change, and the sustainability of agricultural systems. CSA has been defined as “an approach to managing farms and landscapes to enhance food security and resilience in a changing climate”. To ensure that interventions are CSA, they should be planned and implemented in a participatory manner, with the involvement of a broad range of stakeholders. However, there are currently no standardized methods for assessing the CSA-suitability of an intervention. This study aimed to develop and test a participatory method for assessing the CSA-suitability of an agricultural intervention. The study was conducted in Northern Benin, where the research team has been working with small-scale farmers since 2013. The method was developed through a series of focus group discussions and key informant interviews with a broad range of stakeholders. The resulting assessment framework was piloted and fine-tuned in two villages in the region. The results of the pilot study showed that the method was able to generate rich and varied discussions amongst participants, and that it was flexible enough to be adapted to the local context. The assessment framework was structured in two main parts. Tanzania is a country in east Africa with a rapidly growing population of more than 60 million. It is one of the poorest countries in the world with an adult literacy rate of 70% and an average life expectancy of 61 years. The mainstay of the economy is agriculture but 80% of the population depend on subsistence farming. The average annual income per capita is less than US$1,000. Tobacco is the most important cash crop and smoking is the single most important risk factor for oral cancer. The high prevalence of smoking, combined with a lack of access to dental care means that the majority of oral cancers are likely to go undetected until they are at an advanced stage. The aim of this study is to establish the role of potentially etiological agents in oral and oropharyngeal cancer aetiology.
This is a case-control study. Cases will be newly diagnosed patients with biopsied histologically confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity or oropharynx, or with cancer of the lip. Two controls will be selected for each case from the general population, matched by age (±5 years) and gender. Study participants will be recruited from the population attending the Ocean Road Cancer Institute, which serves a referral population of approximately 20 million people. They will be asked a structured questionnaire covering demographic details, dietary and agricultural habits, possible etiological agents, and oral health related issues. In addition, trained researchers will make observations of the home environment of cases and controls. The observations will cover a range of items including the condition of the dwelling, the storage, preparation and cooking of food and the use of pesticides. The study will run for four years, during which time around 500 cases and 1000 controls are planned. The results of this study will be analysed using standard statistical techniques.

This study aimed to identify and prioritise CSA objectives in order to provide guidance for CSA implementation in the Western Cape. A literature study was conducted to identify CSA objectives. An online and paper-based questionnaire was developed to gather information on the perceived importance of the objectives in the Western Cape. The questionnaires were distributed among 300 individuals involved in agricultural production and/or processing in the Western Cape. Respondents were asked to rank the objectives in order of importance. Non-parametric statistical tests were used to investigate differences in the mean rankings of the objectives. The results of the online and paper-based questionnaires were compared and combined to achieve a final ranking of the CSA objectives. A total of 21 objectives were identified in the literature study. The top 10 most important objectives according to the respondents were as follows: maintaining or improving soil health; increasing biodiversity; leaving enough natural vegetation to support wildlife; reducing pesticide use; increasing farmer-to-farmer interaction; leaving enough wildflowers to support insect life; maintaining or improving groundwater quality; reducing or eliminating the use of chemical fertilizers; managing agricultural land to conserve water; and leaving enough trees to support bird life. The results of the ranking exercise showed significant differences for 13 of the 21 objectives (P < 0.05). The objectives that showed the largest differences in mean rankings were ‘improved food security at the household level’ and ‘increased income for farmers’.

A new study led by the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and published in Nature Sustainability has found that using new monitoring techniques to measure ecosystem function can help both scientists and farmers prepare for climate change.

The study, led by U of I crop sciences professor Donald D. Lorenzini, used a combination of remote sensing and in situ measurements to predict how much nitrogen would be needed to maintain a certain level of crop yield.

“Maintaining a certain crop yield requires more nitrogen when the climate is warmer and drier,” Lorenzini said.

The new monitoring techniques allow farmers to maintain a certain crop yield with less nitrogen, reducing the amount of nitrogen fertilizer they need to use while still achieving the desired yield.

The techniques also help scientists better understand the role nitrogen plays in the environment.

“Nitrogen is a limited resource that must be replaced annually,” Lorenzini said. “Too much nitrogen in the environment can lead to eutrophication, which can cause ecosystem stress and even the proliferation of harmful algal blooms.”

By understanding how nitrogen moves through the ecosystem, scientists can develop more effective ways to recycle nitrogen and reduce the amount of nitrogen fertilizer that ends up polluting the environment.

The new monitoring techniques are also a step forward in preparing for the effects of climate change.

“As the climate changes, so does the ecosystem,” Lorenzini said. “By using these techniques to monitor the ecosystem, we can better understand how climate change will affect ecosystem function and prepare for the changes we will see in the years ahead.”

Photo: C. Kozar, CIAT (CC BY-NC-ND 2.0)


A new study published in Nature Sustainability shows that adopting climate-smart agriculture (CSA) practices can help close the gap between the food that is needed, and what is currently produced.

The study, led by German Research Center for Plant Science (MPI-PG), estimates that globally, CSA practices have the potential to increase global grain yields by up to 6% and crop productivity by up to 20%. This could prevent 30% of the decrease in global cereal production by 2050 due to increased temperatures.

The analysis also shows that the greatest potential gains are in South Asia, where multiple CSA practices could boost rice yields by up to 29%. This is followed by Sub-Saharan Africa, where multiple CSA practices could increase maize yields by up to 17%.

The researchers say that in addition to boosting productivity, CSA can help make smallholder farming more resilient to climate change, and ensure food security for the almost one billion people around the world who rely on smallholder agriculture for their livelihoods.

The study highlights the importance of public and private investments in agricultural research to help close the food gap. It also emphasizes the need for further research to improve understanding of the impacts of CSA practices and to harness the synergies among different CSA practices and with other interventions.

Invasions are occurring at an alarming rate and are the second leading cause of extinction worldwide. The rise of human-mediated invasions is primarily driven by transport and trade, although climate change and damage to native habitats are also major factors. The rise of pathogen invasions is a relatively new area of research, and the mechanisms driving the spread of pathogens are not well understood. Here, we use South Africa as a case study to explore the links between pathogens of vertebrate animals and invasive species. We found that the risk of invasion is higher for pathogens with large changes in range size, a short distance between native and non-native ranges, a short generation time, and a short distance between invasion source and recipient sites. The highest risk pathogens are those with the shortest generation time and largest range change. Overall, 59% of the pathogens are at risk of invasion, with the highest risk in the Pseudoscorpiones, with 100% of the pathogens in this group being invasive. We suggest that the high risk of invasion of these pathogens is due to the high number of invasive species in South Africa, the introduction of generalist pathogens with invasions of non-native species, and the transport of pathogens through the trade of invasive species. Our results suggest that with climate change, we should expect to see an increase in the number of pathogen invasions, and that conservation and agricultural practices should mitigate the transport and spread of invasive species to help protect against pathogen invasions.

Here, we review the literature on the introduction, spread and impacts of invasive alien species in aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems, and highlight examples of disease organisms that have caused ecological or economic harm. We found that the study of disease organisms as invasive species has focused almost exclusively on pathogens, with few examples of infectious pathogens or pests. However, parasites were also identified as invasive species that deserve attention, and a broader definition of an invasive alien species as any disease organism that is introduced to a new area could provide a unifying framework for studying this diverse group of organisms. We propose that invasive alien species provide a new research avenue to invasion scientists to study the invasibility of ecosystems by disease organisms, and suggest that the ecological mechanisms behind their invasibility are likely to be different from those underlying invasions by non-native species that lack the organisational complexity of a host–pathogen interaction network.

Source: https://www.news.utoronto.ca

News Release

What scientists know about microscopic invaders that cause disease in South Africa

For release: March 31, 2022

In a new paper published in Nature Reviews Microbiology, scientists from across Canada and South Africa review what is known about the diversity of microbes that cause disease in people, and the impact of these infections in South Africa.

The paper, written by 11 authors, provides an overview of what is known about the microbes that cause disease in people, with a focus on South Africa. The paper was written by researchers from the University of Toronto, the University of British Columbia, the University of Calgary, the University of Ottawa, the South African National Bioinformatics Institute, the KwaZulu-Natal Research Institute for Tropical Diseases, the South African Medical Research Council, the University of Cape Town, and Stellenbosch University.

“Microbes that cause disease in people are diverse, and different microbes cause disease in different parts of the world,” said co-author Dr. Michael Wilson, assistant professor in the Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology at U of T’s Faculty of Medicine and the research institute for sepsis the University of Toronto’s Centre for Global Health Research. “By understanding which microbes cause disease in a particular region, we can prioritize the development of diagnostics, vaccines, and treatments that are most needed in those regions.”

The paper highlights what is known about the diversity of bacteria, viruses, parasites, and fungi that cause disease in people in South Africa. For example, the paper notes that in high-income areas of the world, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae type b are among the bugs most commonly found to cause pneumonia, while in South Africa, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus agalactiae are more common causes of pneumonia.

The authors also discuss the impact of these infections in South Africa. For example, HIV and tuberculosis remain major challenges in South Africa, and malaria remains a problem in areas of South Africa that border Mozambique and Swaziland. However, there is also evidence of the emergence and re-emergence of other infections in South Africa. For example, a resurgence of measles was observed in 2019 following years of low incidence, and there has been a recent increase in the incidence of leptospirosis in KwaZulu-Natal, with 663 confirmed cases between January and August 2021.

This study aimed to evaluate and compare the treatment outcomes of different treatment modalities for odontogenic keratocyst.
A prospective observational cohort study was conducted on patients with odontogenic keratocyst who were treated from January 2019 to December 2020 at the Faculty of Dentistry, University of Malaya. The treatment modalities evaluated included en bloc resection, cryotherapy, and phenolization. The primary outcome was recurrence of odontogenic keratocyst, and the secondary outcomes were complications, recurrence rate, and disease-free interval.
A total of 70 patients were recruited into the study. The mean age of the patients was 43.13 ± 10.22 years old. Among all the treatment modalities, en bloc resection had the highest disease-free interval (P < 0.001) and lowest recurrence rate (P < 0.001). There was no significant difference in the complication rates among the treatment groups (P = 0.594).
Patients with odontogenic keratocyst could be successfully managed with different treatment modalities. En bloc resection provided the best treatment outcome in terms of recurrence rate and disease-free interval.

A team of researchers from the University of Malaya (UM) has suggested a new method to treat a jaw disease known as idiopathic condylar resorption (ICR).

The study was led by Associate Professor Dr. Lai Wai Peng from the UM School of Dental Sciences and was recently published in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery.

Dr. Lai said that ICR is a progressive disease in which the lower jaw shrinks slowly, and often leads to deformity of the face and malfunction of the jaw joint.

He said that current treatment options are controversial and there is no clear consensus on the best approach to treat the condition.

“Although several treatment options are suggested, including surgery, orthodontics and orthognathic surgery, there is level 1 evidence to support their use.

“The main problem is that there is no standard protocol on how to treat ICR. This makes it difficult for clinicians to make evidence-based decisions on the treatment and management of these patients,” Dr. Lai said.

In this study, the researchers reviewed all available literature on ICR and suggested a treatment protocol.

They suggested that treatment should only be started when the disease has reached a certain point and there is clear evidence of progression.

“Clinicians often start treatment too early, which could expose the patient to unnecessary surgery and orthodontic treatment.

“Our proposed protocol suggests a waiting period before starting treatment and this will help to avoid unnecessary treatment,” Dr. Lai said.

The researchers also suggested that orthodontic treatment alone or orthognathic surgery alone is not the best approach to treat ICR.

They suggested a three-phase treatment involving orthodontics, jaw surgery, and a maintenance phase which is the most effective way to treat ICR.

The results will be published in the open access journal BMC Oral Health on 7 May 2013.

Odontogenic cysts and tumors are the most common diseases affecting the jawbone. They account for 70% of all jaw lesions. The majority of these are non-cancerous, but they can be difficult to treat.

OKC is a rare disease that accounts for 2-4% of all odontogenic tumors and cysts. It can be difficult to diagnose as the symptoms overlap with other jaw diseases. Treatment usually involves removing the cyst or tumor, but if the cyst or tumor returns, the patient may require multiple surgeries.

In this study, researchers led by Dr. Rizwan Mohammed from the Prince Philip Hospital in Hong Kong, identified 6 clinical features that could help doctors to distinguish OKC from other jaw diseases. The features include the size and location of the lesion, whether it has invaded other tissues, and whether it contains teeth.

The researchers then searched the literature to find other studies that had investigated the effectiveness of different treatments for OKC. From this, they were able to suggest a treatment algorithm that could help doctors to provide the best treatment for their patients.

Dr Mohammed commented, “This was the first time that studies on OKC have been combined to give strong recommendations for diagnosis and treatment. There are very few diseases where there have been so many studies investigating the effectiveness of different treatments. We hope that our work will help to improve the quality of life for patients with this debilitating disease.”

and adjuvants for vaccine design

The recent outbreak of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV) has been classified as a pandemic by the World Health Organization. There are currently no vaccines available for the treatment of COVID-19. Hence, there is an urgent need to develop vaccines with the ability to induce a protective immune response. In this study, we proposed a computational method to identify potential epitopes and adjuvants for the design of a synthetic SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV vaccine. We used 5 different computational methods to predict HLA class I and HLA class II restricted epitopes for all the available coronavirus proteins from three different coronavirus genera, and subsequently, performed an in silico immunoinformatics analysis to identify potential adjuvants for vaccine design. Our results suggest that this computational approach can be used to rapidly predict epitopes for vaccine design, which can further be experimentally validated for the identification of candidate epitopes and adjuvants for the development of a synthetic coronavirus vaccine.

The SARS-CoV-2 virus enters the cell by binding to the ACE2 receptor. Therefore, the interaction of the RBD with ACE2 plays a key role in the viral entry, infection, and pathogenesis. The scientists extracted the genetic sequences of 24,000 viruses from the virus family that includes Sars and Covid-19. They then compared the sequences to find out which regions of the viruses were likely to be recognized by the immune system and therefore could help the body fight the infection.

Dr Neelanga Kandasamy, from the University of Cambridge’s Sanger Institute, said: “By comparing the genomes of different coronaviruses, we were able to identify regions of the virus which are likely to be recognized by the immune system and could help explain why some people get very ill while others don’t.

“This information could be used to develop new treatments and potentially a vaccine to protect people from future coronaviruses.”

Dr Elrufai Bejesu, from the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, said: “We need to develop new technologies to help us understand how viruses can circulate in humans and animals and how they can adapt to a new environment.

“This will help scientists to find ways to prevent the occurrence and spread of future epidemic viruses.”

The research was published in Nature Microbiology.


The Sanger Institute
The Wellcome Sanger Institute is one of the world’s leading genome centres. The Institute is based at the Wellcome Genome Campus, Hinxton, Cambridge, which is home to over 1,000 people in cutting-edge research, analysis and IT teams supporting hundreds of scientists in the UK and across the globe.

The scientists used a method called phylodynamics to analyze 101 coronavirus genomes from humans and 14 from bats. They found that Covid-19 is most closely related to a coronavirus found in bats in China. They also found that the virus has changed since it first infected humans. The scientists say this is evidence that the virus was initially adapted to bats and then changed as it spread to other animals, including humans.

The study provides evidence that SARS-CoV-2 had an animal reservoir and was not simply passed directly from bats to humans.

The scientists say their findings could help in the development of vaccines and other treatments.

The study was conducted by researchers from the University of Liège in Belgium and several other institutions in Belgium, Mali, Germany, China, the United States and the Netherlands.

It is the first time scientists have compared Covid-19 to two coronaviruses that do not cause disease in humans. The two coronaviruses are HKU1 and MERS.

The scientists say their method of comparing coronaviruses could be used to look for other viruses that might be dangerous to humans.

But the researchers were already working on a new vaccine against a different coronavirus: SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes Covid-19. The new vaccine, called mRNA-1273, was created using messenger RNA (mRNA) that contained instructions for making a piece of a protein found on the surface of the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The protein, called the spike protein, helps the virus attach to and enter human cells. The vaccine then taught the body to fight the virus by recognizing the spike protein as a threat. The vaccine was developed by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), part of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), in collaboration with the biotechnology company Moderna.

The trial was conducted by researchers at Kaiser Permanente Washington Health Research Institute, part of Kaiser Permanente Washington, a managed care organization serving 780,000 lives in Washington state. The team worked with community partners, including the Portland/Seattle COVID-19 Cohort Study, to quickly identify people who were willing to be vaccinated and followed them for a year. Participants were aged 18–55 and were recruited through social media, community groups, and in-person outreach. The study enrolled 45 people in total: 23 in the vaccine group and 22 in the placebo group. All the participants were healthy adults with no known risk factors for developing a severe case of Covid-19. The researchers followed the participants for a median of 14.5 days in the placebo group and 13 days in the mRNA-1273 group. During that time, none of the participants got Covid-19.

The study was conducted by researchers from the Universities of Oxford, Cambridge and Liverpool, and the Medical Research Council (MRC) in the UK, as well as from the University of Tsukuba in Japan. The study was published in Nature Communications on 17 March 2022.

The researchers used a technique called molecular docking to identify areas on the virus that could bind to human immune system proteins. Molecular docking is a method used in computational biology to predict how two molecules will interact with each other. In this case, the researchers were predicting how parts of the Covid-19 virus would interact with parts of the human immune system.

The technique was used to identify six different epitopes on the virus. These epitopes were then tested using a method called a binding assay to confirm that they could indeed bind to human immune system proteins. The binding assay is a test used to measure the affinity between two molecules. In this case, the assay measured the affinity between the epitopes on the virus and the human immune system proteins.

The researchers then tested how well the immune system recognized the different epitopes in a group of healthy human volunteers. They found that all of the epitopes were recognized by the immune system, although some were recognized better than others. This information can be used by vaccine developers to design vaccines that target a wide range of epitopes on the virus, increasing the likelihood that the vaccine will be effective against different variants of Covid-19.

In addition to identifying new epitopes for potential use in vaccines, this study also provides a method that can be used to quickly identify new epitopes on other viruses, such as those that cause flu or Ebola. This could be an important tool for public health officials in responding to future pandemics.

This is a very important feature of the virus because it’s what allows the virus to infect people. This is why scientists around the world are closely monitoring any changes to the virus.

The original SARS-CoV-2 virus that started the pandemic in 2019 had a spike protein that bound very well to the ACE2 receptor found on the surface of human cells. This allowed the virus to latch onto the cell and begin replicating. 

But scientists discovered that there were 92 different mutations in the virus’s spike protein found across all the sequenced SARS-CoV-2 genomes. This was a big surprise because the virus doesn’t usually undergo many changes over a short period of time, even though it replicates very rapidly and infects many people. 

We set out to better understand these mutations and their potential effect on the virus, by investigating how even slight changes in the spike protein affect its ability to bind to the ACE2 receptor. 

We found that a small number of these mutations can significantly affect the interaction between the spike and the ACE2 receptor. In particular, we discovered that four of these mutations, found in different parts of the spike protein, all work together to increase the number of ACE2 receptors that the spike can bind to. 

This means that a virus carrying these four mutations may be able to bind to more of the ACE2 receptors in the body, which would allow it to infect more people. 

It is important to note that a virus needs many other parts of the infection process to be complete, such as infecting other cells, replicating, and causing disease. But a virus that can bind more effectively to human cells is still a big concern and a very important feature for transmission.

We also found that some of these mutations had already been seen in viruses found in patients. One mutation was first detected in Hong Kong in December 2019, just before the pandemic was publicly announced. Another mutation was first detected in Brazil in February 2020. To date, there are at least 92 different genetic variations of SARS-CoV-2 circulating globally, with different combinations of these mutations. 

While these mutations have not significantly changed the interaction between the spike protein and ACE2 receptors, it is possible that a different mutation, or a combination of mutations, could have a more significant effect. For this reason, scientists are continuing to monitor the evolution of the virus.

English:
Cardiac arrhythmias are common in patients with COVID-19. However, it is still unclear whether patients with COVID-19 are at an increased risk of developing arrhythmias. The aim of this study was to evaluate the risk of arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19.
English:
We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort and case-control studies on the risk of arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19.
English:
A total of 4690 patients with COVID-19 from 14 studies were included in the meta-analysis. The incidence of arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19 was 17.8% (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.6%-25.1%). Patients in the ICU had an increased risk of arrhythmias (p < 0.001, CI, 1.01-2.52). The incidence of arrhythmias was higher in patients with COVID-19 during the acute phase (p < 0.001, CI, 1.41-3.18) and in those requiring ICU admission (p < 0.001, CI, 1.59-4.87) compared to patients with COVID-19 during the non-acute phase and those not requiring ICU admission, respectively. ST segment elevation (p < 0.001, CI, 1.92-4.87) and new atrial fibrillation (p < 0.001, CI, 2.40-7.35) were also associated with an increased risk of arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19.
English:
Our findings suggest that patients with COVID-19 are at an increased risk of developing arrhythmias, especially during the acute phase of the disease and in those requiring ICU admission. ST segment elevation and new atrial fibrillation were also associated with an increased risk of arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to investigate whether patients with COVID-19 and arrhythmias would benefit from specific antiarrhythmic drugs.

This study aimed to explore the prevalence and risk factors of cardiac arrhythmia in COVID-19 patients. A retrospective cohort study was conducted based on 169 COVID-19 patients who were admitted to the ICU of a tertiary general hospital in Hubei, China, from January 20 to April 15, 2020. The prevalence, types, and risk factors of cardiac arrhythmia were analyzed. The arrhythmia group was compared with the non-arrhythmia group in terms of clinical characteristics, laboratory examinations, and length of ICU stay and 28-day mortality. A total of 34 (20.10%) patients developed cardiac arrhythmia, and new onset atrial fibrillation (n = 26, 15.88%) was the most common type of arrhythmia. Patients with arrhythmia were significantly older, more likely to be male, had a higher prevalence of comorbidities, higher levels of creatine kinase (CK) and D-dimer, lower levels of lymphocyte (LYM), and lower levels of albumin (ALB) than those without arrhythmia. Multivariate analysis indicated that age (OR 1.07, 95% CI 1.02-1.13, p = 0.005), sex (OR 3.72, 95% CI 1.34-10.26, p = 0.01), and CK (OR 1.01, 95% CI 1.00-1.01, p = 0.01) were independently associated with an increased risk of arrhythmia. Patients with arrhythmia stayed in the ICU for 12 (10-15) days, 4 (2-10) days earlier than those without arrhythmia, and the mortality rate was 47.06% (16/34), which was higher than that of non-arrhythmia patients (18.75%, 6/32), with statistically significant differences (p = 0.01). Cardiac arrhythmia occurs frequently in COVID-19 patients and is associated with worse outcomes. Older patients, males, and those with elevated CK and decreased LYM and ALB levels are at a higher risk of developing arrhythmia. More attention and support are needed to improve the survival rate of these patients.

This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis that aimed to identify and summarize the incidence of cardiac arrhythmia in patients with COVID-19. The following databases were searched from their inception up to 8th of May 2021: PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, Science Direct, Wiley Online Library, Web of Science, ClinicalKey, and Cochrane Library. The search was conducted in two steps. In the first step, the keywords and Mesh terms were searched in all databases. In the second step, the references of all retrieved articles were hand-searched to identify more relevant articles. The search terms are shown in Appendix Table A1-A3. In this study, international studies published as full articles in English language were included; case reports, reviews, and studies published as abstracts, conference proceedings, or news articles were excluded. The selected studies were assessed for methodological quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort studies and the Modified Diamond Style for case-control studies. Data extraction was performed using a standardized collection form. Study characteristics including first author, year of publication, country of origin, sample size, mean age, and proportion of male participants were extracted. The incidence of cardiac arrhythmia was also extracted. Data were pooled using a random effect model and presented as incidence rate per 100 infected individuals with 95% confidence interval (CI). Heterogeneity between studies was assessed using the Cochrane’s Q test and the tau-squared statistic. To evaluate the potential publication bias, a funnel plot was generated and the Egger’s intercept was used. Sensitivity analysis was also performed. Subgroup analysis was conducted to explore the association of cardiac arrhythmia with age, gender, and disease severity. Studies were stratified into two groups by age (<60 years vs. ≥60 years), gender (male vs. female), and disease severity (non-severe vs. severe or critical). The statistical analysis was performed using R software (version 4.1.0) and the meta-analysis was performed using the “metafor” package. This research was supported by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey (grant number: 114S270).

The purpose of this study was to evaluate the ability of the lead I signal in the detection of atrial fibrillation (AF) and flutter (AFl) in comparison to a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG). Methods: In this prospective study, 547 patients with suspected AF or AFl were included. Signals of lead I and a 12-lead ECG were analyzed. The sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value of lead I in comparison to a 12-lead ECG were calculated. Results: Out of 547 patients, 72 had AF and 21 had AFl. The sensitivity and negative predictive value of lead I were 100% and 94.4%, respectively, for AF and 95.2% and 76.9%, respectively, for AFl. The positive predictive value for the diagnosis of AF and AFl was 77.4% and 63.6%, respectively. Conclusion: The lead I signal is useful for the detection of AF and AFl. Its use as a screening tool may avoid the use of a 12-lead ECG and reduce the time required for monitoring in patients with suspected AF or AFl.

Many Covid-19 patients had irregular heartbeats during infection, study finds
Photo: Shutterstock

Related Topics:
Health News

By Healthday Reporter

THURSDAY, March 25, 2021 (HealthDay News)

A new study finds that many people who developed COVID-19 also had an irregular heart rhythm known as an arrhythmia.

The finding doesn't mean that people with a history of heart rhythm problems should panic if they contract the coronavirus, the researchers said.

"It is not yet known whether people with a history of arrhythmias are more likely to develop serious COVID-19 infection or have a more serious course of the disease," said Dr. Jonathan Steinberg. He's a professor of medicine at the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine in Philadelphia.

"There is also no evidence yet that people with COVID-19 are more likely to develop arrhythmias," Steinberg said.

"People with a history of atrial fibrillation should take precautions to avoid COVID-19 infection," Steinberg added in a school news release. "These include social distancing, hand hygiene, and wearing a mask when in public."

For the study, Steinberg's team used electrocardiogram (EKG) technology to assess heart rhythms of 291 patients hospitalized for COVID-19, and 284 people hospitalized for other reasons.

The EKG results showed that 46% of the COVID-19 patients had some type of arrhythmia, most often atrial fibrillation, which is an irregular fast heartbeat.

The other most common arrhythmia among COVID-19 patients was new-onset ventricular tachycardia, which is a fast heart rate that begins in the lower heart chamber (ventricle). It can lead to sudden cardiac arrest.

The arrhythmia rates among patients hospitalized for other reasons weren't available for comparison.

The findings were published online March 24 in the journal Heart Rhythm.

Arrhythmias can cause the heart to work less efficiently, which means the heart may not be able to circulate enough oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body. This can cause heart failure, among other problems.

There is also some evidence that people with heart disease or who have had a heart attack are at higher risk from COVID-19, the researchers noted.

The American Heart Association has more on atrial fibrillation.

We begin by briefly describing the migration patterns of the three main groups of migrants coming to Europe: forced migrants, refugees and economic migrants. We then review the empirical evidence on the mental health and wellbeing of each of these three groups. The evidence suggests that refugees and asylum seekers experience higher levels of psychological distress than economic migrants. This is likely due to the traumatic events that refugees experience or have witnessed (e.g. war, political persecution, torture, and/or mass killing) as well as the uncertainty of their status as refugees waiting for asylum status to be granted. In contrast, forced migrants who are not granted refugee status at the time of the assessment are often subsequently granted refugee status, and thus their psychological distress is more in line with that of refugees. In addition, economic migrants may have left their country due to economic reasons, but they also report high levels of exposure to war and political persecution, and experience multiple push and pull factors, which can impact their mental health and wellbeing. Finally, we discuss the factors that have been found to buffer the negative impact of migration on mental health and wellbeing. In particular, we discuss the protective role of pre-migration social support, migration preparedness, reception conditions, integration, and post-migration social support. The chapter ends with a discussion of methodological issues in migration research, in particular the challenges in measuring mental health and wellbeing, and the appropriate sample for conducting research on the mental health and wellbeing of migrants.

samples.hyp:
However, few studies have examined the relative impact of pre- and post-migration stressors on mental health and PTSD separately in a single sample. This study examined the relative impact of pre- and post-migration stressors on PTSD symptoms in a sample of 337 Syrian refugees and migrants living in Lebanon. Results showed that both pre- and post-migration stressors were significantly associated with PTSD symptoms, even after controlling for potential confounding variables. More specifically, in both unadjusted and adjusted models, pre-migration stressors explained a larger proportion of the variance in PTSD symptoms than post-migration stressors. Limitations of the study include a significant proportion of missing data, the cross-sectional design, the use of self-report measures, and the single-item measures employed for some study variables. The study also drew a sample from one location in Lebanon, so caution is needed when generalizing the results to other locations in Lebanon or other countries hosting Syrian refugees. The location of the study (Beirut and surrounding areas) meant that the sample was particularly exposed to post-migration stressors such as poverty and unemployment. Despite these limitations, this study provides some of the first evidence of the relative impact of pre- and post-migration stressors on PTSD symptoms in Syrian refugees and migrants. Future research should employ larger, more generalizable samples, longitudinal designs, multiple assessment methods, and more comprehensive measures of pre- and post-migration stressors.

samples.hyp:
The situation in a refugee’s home country and the process of settling in a new place are associated with mental health problems among refugees, according to a review of more than 30 studies from around the world, published in the British Medical Journal today.

The studies showed that refugees were more likely to have symptoms of depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and psychosis. Refugees were also more likely to have thought about and attempted suicide.

Dr. Cathryne Ng-Mosha, from the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Maryland, USA, who led the review, said: “The situation in a refugee’s home country and the process of resettling in a new place are associated with mental health problems among refugees. There are many factors that may contribute to this, including loss, social isolation, difficulty adjusting to a new culture, and discrimination.”

Dr. Ng-Mosha added: “It is important for health professionals to be aware of the mental health issues that refugees may face and to provide appropriate services and care.”

In this review, the researchers grouped the studies by the situation in the refugee’s home country and the time since the person fled their home. They found that the strength of the associations between being a refugee and mental health problems differed according to these two factors.

Refugees from countries affected by armed conflict had particularly high rates of mental health problems, while refugees from countries affected by human rights violations had particularly high rates of PTSD. The researchers suggest that this may be due to the unique nature of these types of human rights violations.

Refugees who had been in their new country for a short time (up to 5 years) were more likely to have thought about suicide, while those who had been there longer (10 to 30 years) were more likely to have attempted suicide. The researchers suggest that this may be due to an initial period of high stress immediately after arrival, followed by an adjustment period, during which symptoms of depression remit, but risk of suicide may increase.

They point out that the studies had some methodological problems, and that the findings may not be representative of all refugees, so more research is needed.

Dr. Ng-Mosha said: “It is important for health professionals to be aware of the mental health issues that refugees may face and to provide appropriate services and care. This is especially important as the number of refugees worldwide continues to rise.”

In subsistence farming, the competition is reduced because the farmer relies on his own capital, labour, and the products from his own farm for sustenance. The own resources of the farmer in subsistence farming are not only a threat to national food security but are also a guarantee for the same. Heartwater is a tick-borne disease of livestock and wildlife caused by the protozoan parasite, Cardia Boldia. The disease is characterized by a febrile illness with variable degrees of anorexia, depression, and somnolence that may last for several weeks. The pathogen is transmitted by the brown ear tick, Rhipicephalus evertsi, and spread through direct contact with infected ticks or contaminated blood or tissues. The study was conducted in two villages in the Tuli Block of the Central District of Botswana. A total of 1080 animals comprising 648 cattle, 432 goats, and 252 sheep were examined between March and November 2007. In addition, 1200 sheep were vaccinated in September 2007. The overall prevalence of heartwater was 16.2% (176/1080) with a confidence interval of 13.3-19.0%. Prevalence was higher in goats (21.0%) than in cattle (16.3%) and sheep (8.7%). The mean ± SD age of seropositive animals was 2.2 ± 2.2 years for cattle, 1.6 ± 1.5 years for goats, and 1.9 ± 1.8 years for sheep. The adult tick population peaked in April and then declined throughout the study period. The prevalence of heartwater in vaccinated and unvaccinated animals was 3.3% (4/120) and 17.9% (156/870), respectively. There was no significant difference (P > 0.05) in the prevalence of heartwater between the two villages. In conclusion, the study revealed a public health problem in the Tuli Block of Botswana, where heartwater is highly prevalent in livestock. The disease is stable in the tuli area and vaccination is not effective due to poor immunization coverage. The findings highlight the need for effective control strategies, which should include measures to improve animal health and tick control through integrated parasite management and ecological methods.

Ticks are blood-sucking parasites that can transmit diseases to livestock, such as heartwater. (©iStock)

High numbers of ticks in southern Botswana have led to a rise in heartwater disease in livestock, according to a new study published in the Journal of Economic Entomology.

Heartwater is a debilitating and often fatal disease in animals caused by the protozoan parasite, Cardiaboldes elonia (Apicomplexa: Theileriidae), which is transmitted by the brown ear tick, Rhipicephalus everti (Acari: Ixodidae).

The disease is a constraint to livestock production in sub-Saharan Africa, with losses attributed to weight loss, decreased milk production, and death.

A team of researchers from Botswana, South Africa, and the United States sought to determine the risk of heartwater infection in Botswana, and the role of ticks in transmitting the disease.

They collected 799 ticks from 10 locations in Botswana between January 2019 and October 2020. Of these, 30.1% were adult brown ear ticks, 53.7% were nymphs, and 16.2% were larvae.

The researchers tested the ticks for the presence of heartwater, and found that 5.6% of the adult ticks and 1.9% of the nymphs were positive for the disease.

“[Our] results suggest that the level of heartwater infection in ticks in southern Botswana is low,” write the researchers. “However, the high abundance of ticks, especially the adult brown ear ticks, is a cause for concern because it increases the risk of transmission of heartwater to livestock in the region.”

The researchers also tested the blood of 894 cattle from three locations in Botswana for the presence of heartwater antibodies. One hundred and seventy-one (19.2%) of the cattle were positive for the disease.

The team’s findings suggest that the high abundance of ticks in the southern part of Botswana is the main risk factor for the spread of heartwater disease to livestock in the region.

“The high prevalence of infective ticks, especially the adult brown ear ticks, and the high seroprevalence observed in cattle in the Kalahari are cause for concern and may adversely impact livestock production in the region,” they write.

Heartwater is a tick-borne disease of livestock and wildlife caused by the spirochaete Ehrlichia ruminantium. The disease is characterized by sudden death with a mortality rate of up to 100%. Heartwater is endemic in most sub-Saharan African countries, but importation of infected animals has led to outbreaks in countries previously considered free from the disease, such as Botswana. The main objective of this study was to determine the seroprevalence and risk factors for heartwater in cattle and wildlife in the southern districts of Botswana. A cross-sectional study was conducted from March to December 2014 in cattle and wildlife. Blood samples were collected from 339 cattle and 154 giraffes, zebras, and wildebeests from five districts in the south of Botswana. These districts have previously experienced heartwater outbreaks. Seroprevalence was determined using a competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. A multivariable logistic regression was used to identify risk factors for positive serology in cattle and wildlife. The overall seroprevalence for E. ruminantium was 5.3% (n = 18) in cattle and 8.5% (n = 13) in wildlife. For cattle, risk factors for E. ruminantium seropositivity were tested and zebu breed (adj. OR 8.94, 95% CI 2.26–35.52, p = 0.000) and presence of ticks (adj. OR 7.83, 95% CI 2.53–24.07, p = 0.000) were found to be significant. For wildlife, being a giraffe had a significantly decreased risk of being seropositive (adj. OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.04–0.67, p = 0.01). This study revealed an endemic status of heartwater in the southern districts of Botswana. The detection of E. ruminantium antibodies in wildlife species such as giraffes suggests that these species can act as reservoirs for the infection. The identification of risk factors for the infection in cattle such as zebu breed and the presence of ticks can be used to develop strategies for heartwater control in the country.

Heartwater disease causes millions of dollars in losses for Nigerian farmers

The researchers said heartwater affected local goats and cattle breeds more than breeds from other countries. (photo: Pixabay)

Nigerian farmers suffer millions of dollars in losses due to heartwater disease, which is caused by the parasite, Cardiasina spp., and transmitted by the Amblyomma variegatum tick, according to a new study published in Transboundary and Emerging Diseases.

The disease is geographically restricted to sub-Saharan Africa, where it causes major economic losses for livestock farmers due to abortion in livestock and reduced weight gain in animals that survive.

In the new study, researchers from Nigeria and Germany sought to compare the susceptibility and pathogenicity of Cardiasina spp. between indigenous Nigerian goats and cattle, and Swiss Alpine goats and European cattle.

They exposed groups of young goats and cattle to infestations of the Amblyomma variegatum tick and then monitored them for heartwater disease.

They found that all the imported animals – Swiss goats and European cattle – survived the two-year experiment, while only a third of the indigenous Nigerian animals survived. All the indigenous animals developed heartwater, as shown by the presence of Cardiasina spp. in the bloodstream and heart lesions in the infected animals.

The researchers say the high pathogenicity of the parasite in the indigenous animals can be explained by their lack of exposure to the parasite.

“Cardiasina spp. has a low prevalence in imported goats and cattle, which may be due to previous exposure to the parasite in their country of origin,” the researchers wrote in their study.

“The low prevalence of Cardiasina spp. in these animals could also be due to the fact that they were kept in a tick-free environment before the start of the experiment,” they added.
