The study was conducted by researchers at the University of Botswana, the University of Pretoria in South Africa, and the U.S. Department of Defense's Global Emerging Infections Surveillance and Response System.


The researchers used data from 2007 to 2018 from the Botswana Ministry of Agriculture's surveillance of heartwater in livestock. They also used data from tick surveys conducted throughout the country during that same time. The team then built an environmental suitability map for Amblyomma variegatum, the tick species that can transmit the heartwater bacteria. They then analyzed the relationship between the suitability map and the reported heartwater cases.


The researchers found that reported heartwater cases were more common in areas of the country where the map showed the tick's environment was suitable for survival. The map also showed that parts of the country that were once suitable year-round became less suitable during the dry season. That could explain why, according to the researchers, less than 5% of the reported heartwater cases occurred between May and October, which is the country's dry season. Amos Tshegetsang, a veterinarian and a researcher at the University of Botswana's Department of Clinical Studies, says the findings will help inform future surveillance and control methods for heartwater in livestock. "It will help us to know that in areas which are highly suitable, we should probably increase the intensity of surveillance," Tshegetsang says. "We may also want to look at possible control measures, such as treatment of animals with acaricides, in those areas highly suitable all year round." The researchers say the map could also help predict where future heartwater outbreaks may occur. Tshegetsang says additional research is needed to confirm that. "Our map shows the general distribution of the tick and where it can survive," Tshegetsang says. "It does not show us the dynamics of the tick, how the tick is actually moving around from one host to another." He says more research is needed to understand more about how the tick is distributed in Botswana. Such research could help scientists develop better ways to predict where future heartwater outbreaks might occur. This story was produced by SciDev.Net’s African Network. Point of care testing (POCT) is a diagnostic strategy with the aim to bring laboratory testing closer to the site of patient care, and ultimately the patient themselves. POCT can improve health outcomes and patient management by reducing the time to result, enabling clinicians to reach a diagnosis and/or management decision earlier. POCT can also provide patients with greater involvement in their own healthcare, empowering them to make decisions about their treatment and care. There are a number of different POCT platforms available, for example, lateral flow assays (immunochromatography) such as the SD Bioline HIV 1/2 (Fig. 1) which detect antibodies to HIV-1 and HIV-2, and the OraQuick HIV Self-Test which is a rapid, oral-based POCT for the detection of HIV-1 and HIV-2. POCTs are also available for the detection of a range of other disease states including malaria (e.g. SD Bioline Malaria Rapid Test which uses a combination of monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies to detect the malaria antigen Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein-II), hepatitis B (e.g. SD Bioline HBsAg Rapid Test which uses a double antigen sandwich technique to detect antibodies to the hepatitis B surface antigen), syphilis (e.g. SD Bioline Syphilis Rapid Test which uses a double antigen sandwich technique to detect antibodies to recombinant treponema pallidum N40 and T. pallidum polypeptide II), and Zika (e.g. SD Bioline Zika Rapid Test which uses an antigen-capture sandwich technique to detect antibodies to the Zika virus).

The test’s accuracy, the ability to interpret the test results, and the ability to take the test in the field are also critical factors. The test’s accuracy is related to the test’s sensitivity and specificity. The test’s sensitivity is the ability of the test to correctly identify those with the target condition. The test’s specificity is the ability of the test to correctly identify those without the target condition. Ideally, a test would have 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity, indicating that the test is able to correctly identify all those with the target condition and none of those without the target condition. However, this is usually not the case, and there is often a trade-off between the two. For example, a test with a high sensitivity may have a low specificity, meaning that it may incorrectly identify some individuals as having the target condition when they do not. Conversely, a test with a high specificity may have a low sensitivity, meaning that it may fail to identify some individuals as having the target condition when they do. The ability to interpret the test results is also crucial. The test results must be easy to interpret, and healthcare workers must be trained to correctly interpret the results. Otherwise, the test may be of limited use. For example, if the test results are difficult to interpret, healthcare workers may misinterpret the results, leading to incorrect diagnoses and inappropriate treatment. Finally, the ability to take the test in the field is also critical. The test must be simple to use and require minimal training and equipment. Otherwise, the test may not be feasible in resource-limited settings. In conclusion, the availability of cheap, simple, and rapid tests outside laboratories is an important step towards successful POC testing. However, the accuracy of the test, the ability to interpret the test results, and the ability to take the test in the field are also critical factors that must be considered to ensure the success of POC testing.

This is the aim of the Diagnostics at the Point of Care (DPC) research network, a new collaborative research network funded by the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Invention for Innovation (i4i) Programme. The network is a collaboration between three leading UK universities (Sheffield, Newcastle and Imperial) and nine NHS organisations, with industrial partners Abbott and Roche, and the devolved nations (Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland).  

The network will focus on three key areas:

  1. Understanding the role of POC diagnostics in the management of patients in very urgent care (e.g. emergency department, major trauma) and urgent care (e.g. out of hours primary care, rapid transfer teams) pathways.
  2. Understanding the role of POC diagnostics in the management and treatment of chronic diseases in community settings such as general practice, ambulatory care, and care at home.
  3. Enabling the use of digital health technologies (e.g. telehealth, wearables, and electronic patient records) to support the introduction of new POC diagnostic devices, and to facilitate the sharing of data for network research.

There is a lack of understanding about how best to use the growing range of POC diagnostics. The network will address this by undertaking applied health research, and by implementing and evaluating new POC diagnostic devices. The aim is to increase uptake of new POC diagnostics into healthcare, and to ensure that NHS patients benefit from new and emerging technologies.

The researchers say that the study is the first to look at the actual use of HIV testing in a resource-constrained setting. "The results show that the HIV testing process is not as simple as just going to a clinic and getting tested," says Dr. Heidi Hoyle, who conducted the study as part of her PhD thesis at the Nuffield Department of Primary Health Care - Health Sciences, University of Oxford. "The study highlights the importance of understanding the practicalities of implementing HIV testing in resource-constrained settings, in order to make the process run smoothly. This includes understanding the logistics of how patients make appointments, how they get to the clinic and why some patients don't show up for their appointments." For the study, the Oxford researchers worked with the Medecins Sans Frontiers (MSF) clinic in Cape Town. HIV testing is done in two stages: the first stage is a finger-prick test that shows whether the patient should proceed to the second stage, which is a blood test. At the MSF clinic, patients are referred to a central testing site, which is staffed by MSF nurses, and where results are available within 15 minutes. The testing site is located away from the main clinic, which meant patients had to make two separate appointments, and could potentially face long wait times if the central testing site was busy. The researchers observed 175 patients who were referred to the testing site and followed them up to find out why some were not present for their second appointment. They found that 14% of patients did not show up for their second appointment. Those who did not show up were either the ones who had tested negative in the first stage and did not want to go through the second, more invasive stage, or they had tested positive in the first stage and did not want to go through the second stage in case they would get their results and have to wait for treatment. The researchers also found that 40% of patients had to show another identity document at the testing site, as the MSF clinic did not have their details on file. This was because the patients had used a different identity card to the one they had used when booking their appointment. : A systematic review

Background: The concepts of critical illness and critical care are used frequently in health care practice and research. Despite their importance, no formal definitions of these concepts have been developed. The lack of formal definitions creates problems for information retrieval, health services research, and health care education. Concept analysis, a component of ontology science, provides a method for defining concepts. The goal of this paper is to conduct a systematic review of the literature to identify the published papers that used concept analysis to develop definitions of critical illness and critical care. The results will be used to conduct a concept analysis of these terms. Methods: The search strategy was designed to identify English-language papers that reported the use of concept analysis to develop definitions of critical illness and critical care and included publications from January 1, 1980 to December 31, 2013. The search was performed in PubMed, CINAHL, and Ebsco host. The reference lists of papers were also reviewed to identify additional publications that met the criteria. Results: The literature search identified 17 papers. The papers were evaluated for methodological quality. The majority of the papers were found to have serious flaws in their methods. Conclusion: The literature search identified a limited number of papers that used concept analysis to develop definitions of critical illness and critical care. The quality of these studies was poor. There is a need to conduct new studies of these concepts using concept analysis. This will help to develop formal definitions of these concepts.

Experts were defined as having published on the topic of FHR assessment in the last 5 years or having more than 50 published articles on the topic of FHR assessment. The online survey was distributed to the members of the EFC, an international organization of clinical professionals with a primary focus on fetal heart rate assessment, and additional experts were referred by respondents. The survey was distributed in June 2019, and responses were collected over a 6-month period. Experts were asked about their role, country of work, number of years since completion of their medical training, and number of publications on FHR assessment. They were asked to rate the importance of 21 concepts related to FHR monitoring and to define the meaning of 8 terms that were unclear or had multiple meanings. Expert definitions were analyzed using inductive content analysis to identify common themes. The Delphi method was used to achieve consensus on the final set of definitions.
Conclusion
The findings of this study support the EFC’s decision to include an FHR education module in their global curriculum. The definitions provided here could be used by educators, researchers, and regulatory bodies to standardize terminology and promote clear communication in FHR research and clinical practice. This study has several limitations. First, expert opinion may not be representative of all clinical perspectives. Second, although our survey was distributed worldwide, our sample may not be representative of all clinical settings. Third, because this was the first Delphi study on the language of FHR, our survey included 21 concepts for rating and 8 terms for definition. In a subsequent study, we recommend reducing the number of concepts and terms for greater efficiency. Despite these limitations, this study provides a foundation for future research on the language of FHR and could help to facilitate communication about FHR among clinicians worldwide.

We suggest a set of core outcomes and core elements of care for PUD, and provide a preliminary classification of PUD severity. We suggest that the core elements of care for PUD should include: 1) patient education about PUD, its complications, and how to prevent progression of the disease; 2) haemostatic therapy for acute bleeding episodes; 3) maintenance therapy to prevent rebleeding; 4) treatment of underlying aetiology; 5) nutritional support; and 6) psychosocial support. We suggest that the minimum core outcomes to be measured in patients with PUD should include: 1) presence of haematochezia or haematemesis; 2) need for transfusion; 3) rebleeding; 4) development of complications; 5) length of hospital stay; and 6) 30-day and 90-day mortality. We suggest a preliminary classification of PUD severity based on aetiology, presence of haematochezia or haematemesis, need for transfusion, and development of complications. This article provides a foundation from which to build an integrated care approach, and to develop a core outcome set and measurement tool for future use in clinical practice, quality improvement, and research of patients with PUD.

English:
This concept analysis is the first study to systematically describe the uses and definitions of the concepts critical illness and critical care. The Walker and Avant concept analysis model was used. Data were collected from a literature search of the terms critical illness and critical care in CINAHL, Medline, and Google Scholar. The "best" definition of critical illness was determined by the use of a modified Walker and Avant concept analysis. Critical care was determined by a Delphi panel. Critical illness was found to be a state of acute severe disease, present for less than 24 hours, that is life-threatening. Critical care was found to be a level of nursing care given to a patient with an acute illness or injury that is life-threatening and requires constant monitoring and support of vital vital functions. Critical illness and critical care are distinct concepts. Critical care is the nursing specialty that cares for patients with critical illness. Critical illness and critical care are necessary for the nursing profession.

The human malaria parasite Plasmodium develops in liver cells during infection and induces dramatic changes in the cellular morphology of the host. Altered microtubule (MT) organization is a key feature of these changes, but the role of MT dynamics in the infection is not fully understood. Here, we used a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen to identify cellular processes that are required for P. berghei liver stage development. We identified 144 genes essential for this stage, 68 of which have not been described as essential for the blood stage, highlighting the cell biological differences between these two stages. We experimentally validated the top hit of this screen, centrin phosphatase J (CENPJ), which is essential for MT dynamics in multiple eukaryotes. Analysis of human liver biopsies from P. falciparum-infected patients revealed that CENPJ localizes to the parasite-containing vacuole (PCV) and is recruited to the infected cell periphery. In P. berghei-infected human hepatoma cells, CRISPR-Cas9 deletion of the homologous gene, PbCENPJ, impairs MT polymerization and alters the characteristic changes in cell morphology induced by infection. These results identify CENPJ as a component of the host MT network that is directly involved in regulating the altered MT organization induced by the parasite during infection.

Keywords: CRISPR-Cas9, malaria, Plasmodium, liver stage, microtubules, CENPJ, centrin phosphatase J.

Short Summary
The human malaria parasite Plasmodium infects liver cells and induces dramatic changes in their morphology. Here, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen and identify the centrin phosphatase J (CENPJ) as a key regulator of the altered microtubule (MT) organization induced by Plasmodium during infection. We also provide a characterization of the essential genes of the malaria parasite during its initial stages in the human liver.

However, the specific resources targeted by Plasmodium and their role in merozoite development is unknown. Using a combination of mass spectrometry and quantitative immunofluorescence, we identified 144 host proteins that are significantly (P < 0.05) enriched in infected hepatocytes. Of these, 105 proteins are localized in the peroxisomes and 44 are secreted proteins. Further analysis of these proteins by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) identified 78 proteins as specific Plasmodium targets. Plasmodium target proteins are involved in a range of processes, including protein folding, the unfolded protein response, protein turnover, and autophagy. To test the role of these host proteins in merozoite development, we used RNA interference to knock down their expression in the liver stage of Plasmodium berghei. Depletion of host proteins with homology to uncharacterized Plasmodium targets had no effect on parasite growth. In contrast, depletion of peroxiredoxin 2 (PRDX2) reduced P. berghei replication by 38%, and RNA interference of PRDX2 in the human parasite P. falciparum reduced Plasmodium growth by 40% in patient-derived hepatocytes. The data identify PRDX2 as a key host target of Plasmodium that is important for growth in both mammalian and human cells.

This dynamic organization is dependent on the presence of the parasite and is distinct from that of the host cytoskeleton. The host microtubule plus ends preferentially nucleate actin filaments in the parasite, suggesting that the microtubules may organize the filamentous/actin-based motility system of the parasite. We also show that the parasite prevents the microtubules from growing towards the parasite cell membrane. These findings suggest that the LS parasite may exploit host microtubules to organize its own motility system, redirect host microtubule growth, or both.

We found that knockdown of host genes encoding proteins essential for lipid biogenesis, such as FBN1, DHRS3, and NR5A2, reduced LS development. We also found that LRBA, FBN1, and DHRS3 affect the lipid species composition on the plasma membrane. We hypothesize that these proteins alter the plasma membrane properties to regulate invasion. We demonstrate that MTOCs are translocated to the plasma membrane in S. aureus and Rickettsia parkeri infected cells. This translocation is dependent on the actin cytoskeleton and the small GTPase, Rab8. Live cell imaging of MTOCs in conjunction with low temperature electron tomography suggest that MTOCs are externalized by a bud neck microtubule capture mechanism. Thus, bacteria induce the exposure of MTOCs to the plasma membrane in a GTPase dependent manner. Since MTOCs function as an organizing center for the cytoskeleton, we hypothesized that externalization of MTOCs may also modulate the host actin cytoskeleton. Indeed, we find that MTOC translocation is required for the recruitment of F-actin to the plasma membrane and the formation of an actin-rich membrane protrusion, similar to cell motility. This protrusion is dependent on Arp2/3, Cdc42 and formin, and drives bacterial internalization. We conclude that a program of regulated translocation and assembly of MTOCs promotes bacterial internalization and that MTOC externalization may represent a general mechanism of pathogenesis triggered by infection that is conserved in eukaryotes.

Scientists have long known that malaria parasites hijack red blood cells to survive and spread. Now they have mapped out the molecular details of this relationship, a discovery that could help in the development of new treatments.

Malaria is caused by a parasite that’s transmitted to people through the bites of infected mosquitoes. It causes symptoms including fever and headaches, and can be fatal.

The parasite enters the body through the bloodstream and infects red blood cells, multiplying within them. Infected red blood cells then break down, releasing the parasites. These go on to infect more red blood cells.

This means the parasite depends on red blood cells to survive, but the cells are damaged in the process.

There are a number of different types of malaria parasite, and they affect different parts of the world. The most deadly is Plasmodium falciparum, which is prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa.

Until now, it’s not been understood how some types of red blood cells are more susceptible to infection than others. Now, researchers at the University of Oxford have discovered how the parasite binds to red blood cells, and how this can change the cells’ properties.

The parasite uses an enzyme called PIH to bind to a sugar molecule found on red blood cells. This helps it to invade the cell.

The researchers, whose work is published today in Nature Communications, found that PIH also acts as an anti-freeze to protect the parasite as it invades.

Red blood cells stick together in tiny clumps, and the spaces between them are filled with a liquid similar to anti-freeze.

When the parasite first binds to a red blood cell, it switches on a gene called HRP1, which produces a surface protein that acts as an anti-freeze. This stops the protein sticking to the cell, allowing it to move to the next one.

The parasite then injects an enzyme called PI enzyme into the red blood cell. This helps it to change the cell’s structure so that it can take in enough of the parasite to infect it.

The change in structure also makes the cell stickier, which helps the parasite to clump red blood cells together. This is a key part of the disease process, as red blood cells clumping up can cause blockages in the blood vessels.

The researchers found that in some types of red blood cell, the change in structure isn’t as extreme, and the cell isn’t as sticky. This means the parasite can’t clump cells together as effectively, so the disease doesn’t progress as quickly.

The most effective way to prevent malaria is to stop the mosquito that carries the malaria parasite from biting people. The most common mosquito control methods are insecticide spraying and use of mosquito nets. However, mosquitoes are developing resistance to the insecticides, and people are starting to under-use the nets. These observations have prompted the search for new ways of protecting people from mosquito bites.

The salivary glands of male and female mosquitoes contain cells which produce bioactive compounds that are injected along with the mosquito's saliva during a bite. These compounds act in the mosquito's favour, by reducing inflammation and blood clotting, to ensure a smooth blood meal. However, these compounds could also have anti-microbial effects, such as inhibiting the mosquito's own microbes or the transmission of the malaria parasite to the mosquito's next blood meal. In this review, we discuss how such "regurgitation blocking" effects, if strong enough, could provide protection to people from mosquito bites. We describe studies which suggest that certain mosquito blood meals contain molecules that interfere with the regurgitation process and provide an idea of the sort of molecules that could be used as the basis for a new type of long-lasting mosquito repellent.

samples.hyp: South Africa is a signatory to the Global Change Research Programme (GCRP) of the International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP). The GCRP is a core project of the IGBP and aims to (1) understand the global system that is responsive to natural and human-driven global change; (2) assess the magnitude of global change; (3) predict global change in the future, and (4) develop solutions for global change. The GCRP has been implemented through a number of core projects and international projects, such as the IGBP Data and Information System (IDIS), the Biodiversity Synthesis and Analysis Programme (BIOS), and the Land Use/Land Cover Change Programme (LUCCC). South Africa has been involved in all of these projects, and is currently implementing the BIOS and LUCCC projects. The BIOS project has a number of national components, of which the National Biodiversity Invasions Project (NBIP) is one. The NBIP is a collaborative effort between the South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) and the Centre for Ecological Research at the University of KwaZulu-Natal, and focuses on plant invasions. The NBIP has three primary aims: (1) to determine the extent and impact of plant invasions in South Africa; (2) to predict the risk of future plant invasions; and (3) to develop and implement management strategies for preventing plant invasions. The NBIP research is focused on terrestrial and freshwater systems, and has two primary components: (1) a biodiversity component that determines the extent and impact of plant invasions, using both species and ecosystem perspectives; and (2) an invasions component that predicts the risk of future plant invasions and develops and implements management strategies for preventing plant invasions. The NBIP research also has a number of international collaborations, including the Global Invasive Species Programme (GISP), the Invasive Species Specialist Group (ISSG) of the World Conservation Union (IUCN), and the Invasive Species Coalition (ISC) of the USA. The NBIP research contributes to the GCRP through its work on plant invasions. We identified 688 papers that focused on biological invasions (16%), climate change (19%), overharvesting (12%), habitat change (14%), pollution (16%), and atmospheric CO2 (23%). The number of publications increased over time, with a fourfold increase in the number of publications relating to climate change and a twofold increase in the number of publications relating to biological invasions. The fields of biological invasions, climate change, and pollution had the highest number of publications in the Cape Floral Kingdom, the fynbos biome, which is one of the world’s six floral hotspots and one of the planet’s 36 biodiversity hotspots. The greatest number of publications relating to overharvesting were in the Succulent Karoo biome, one of South Africa’s four biomes. The greatest number of publications relating to habitat change were in the grasslands, savanna, and thornveld biomes. Our results show that the South African ecosystems are threatened by a variety of direct and indirect drivers of change, and highlight the need for urgent and sustained research to develop and apply effective management interventions to safeguard South Africa’s biodiversity.

First, the multicausal nature of many health and safety risks means that changes to one driver may shift risk to other drivers. Third, some interactions can be non-linear, such that a small change in one driver can lead to a major change in another. Fourth, management interventions to mitigate risk from one driver can induce risks from other drivers, creating a risk transfer, not a risk reduction. Finally, our ability to model and predict the emergence of risk is limited by our poor understanding of some interaction effects and by the lack of data on the evolution of some drivers.

We reviewed the literature on the interactions between invasive species and other agents that affect ecosystem services in order to identify knowledge gaps and recommend research. We focused on interactions among invasive plants, animals, and pathogens, and between these and biotic and abiotic agents that affect the services provided by species, populations, and ecosystems. We found 118 relevant studies that quantified or qualitatively described interactions between at least two agents that affect the same service in the same ecosystem. Studies focused on biotic agents were dominated by interactions between plants and animals (70%), especially seed dispersal (34%). Studies focusing on the effects of pathogens on services were dominated by plant pathogens (72%) that reduce seed number and quality. We found large knowledge gaps, especially in understanding how multiple agents interact and in drawing conclusions about complex systems. We suggest new research directions to improve our understanding of how multiple agents interact and how these interactions affect services and management of ecosystems.

A new study led by the University of Cape Town (UCT) has found that invasive species, climate change and human activities are all contributing to the degradation of South Africa’s ecosystems, and that these pressures are increasing. The study has highlighted the need for research that maps the combined effect of multiple stressors, such as these, which are often hard to predict on their own.

They found that climate change was likely to favour 42% of these species, with increases in the suitable habitat (i.e. habitat in which the species can survive) of 17%. 
The other papers, by researchers at the University of Queensland, focused on Australia.
One paper looked at how changes in land use — such as urbanisation, agriculture and grazing — have affected the distribution of invasive plants in the country. 
It used field data, satellite imagery and species distribution modelling to show that urbanisation reduced the habitat of native plants by 43%, whereas agriculture and grazing actually increased it by 23%. 
The researchers say their results suggest that invasive plants are more likely to become established in areas that have been affected by land-use change, so managing invasive plants on remnant native vegetation will not be enough to prevent their spread. 
The second paper modelled the potential spread of the invasive giant reed, Arundo donax, in south-east Queensland. 
It found that this species could invade up to 44% of the region if not managed, and that the likelihood of invasion increased the closer the native vegetation was to urban areas. 
The researchers suggest that high priority should be given to managing A. donax along the urban fringe.
The final paper, by researchers at the University of Queensland and the University of Western Australia, modelled the potential spread of the invasive common reed, Phragmites australis, following the removal of native vegetation in south-western Australia. 
It used a combination of field data, satellite imagery and species distribution modelling to show that the area of suitable habitat for P. australis increased after the removal of native vegetation. 
The researchers suggest that this increase in suitable habitat, combined with the presence of water impoundments in the region, poses a high risk of P. australis invasion. 
They advise that in order to prevent or delay this invasion, the most effective control methods should be applied as soon as native vegetation is cleared for agricultural or residential development.

samples.hyp:
In the tropics, SOM is often low and a significant amount of the organic matter input from litter is not retained in the ecosystem. We studied the effect of different litter input and decomposition pathways on SOM in two long-term litter manipulation experiments in the tropical montane forest of Puerto Rico and the tropical lowland rainforest of French Guiana. In Puerto Rico, we incubated SOM with and without leaf litter after wet and dry seasons, and found that litter did not have a significant effect on SOM. In French Guiana, we compared base soil and the O horizons of these soils incubated with and without 15 years of monthly litter addition. We found that the addition of litter increased the amount of potentially mineralizable carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) in the O horizon but not in the mineral soil. These results suggest that the effect of litter on SOM is small in the tropics and that the major factor regulating the amount of litter retained in the ecosystem is decomposition rather than the input amount. Our results also suggest that the main effect of long-term monthly litter addition is to increase the amount of decomposing litter rather than to increase the quantity of SOM. This is likely due to the fact that the monthly litter addition is not large enough to saturate the decomposition pool or to change the quality of the mineral soil pool.

This study aimed to: i) Examine the biogeographic patterns of SOM and C variability in miombo woodlands ii) Quantify the relationship between soil properties, vegetation community and SOM and C pools across a range of land-uses in miombo woodlands.

Soil samples were collected from 27 sites across a range of land-uses in miombo woodland in South Africa and analysed for soil organic carbon (SOC), total nitrogen (N), total organic carbon and nitrogen (TOCN), light fraction carbon (LFC), heavy fraction carbon (HFC) and clay content. Non-parametric statistics and ordination analysis were used to assess biogeographic patterns of soil properties and soil organic matter pools while linear regression was used to quantify relationships.

SOC storage was positively related to clay content and total N, while LFC and HFC were positively related to TOCN and total N. The dominant land-uses were the best predictors of the variability in SOM and C pools, which were ordered in the gradient of increasing land-use intensity: protected areas > ranchland > cropland.

This study highlights the importance of land-use history in understanding SOM and C variability in miombo woodlands. Management of miombo woodland should consider the land-use history of the area for effective C sequestration measures. The study also highlights the need for further research on the effects of land uses such as mining and infrastructure development on SOM and C dynamics in miombo woodlands.

Keywords: Soil organic carbon; soil organic matter; clay content; biogeography; vegetation-Soil relationship

These factors were tree cover, tree density, tree basal area, litter, including leaf litter and fine woody debris (FWD), coarse woody debris (CWD) density, soil moisture content, soil temperature at 5 cm depth and soil pH. Multiple linear regression analysis showed that SOM variability was significantly (P < 0.05) related to tree cover (R2 = 0.35), tree density (R2 = 0.16) and CWD density (R2 = 0.12). The positive relationship between SOM and tree cover is consistent with the findings of other studies that reported increased SOM with increasing tree cover. This finding is also consistent with the view that increased tree cover leads to increased litter input (which is an important source of SOM) and decreased disturbance and soil erosion. The significant relationship between SOM and CWD density could be explained by the fact that CWD input provides carbon and N to the soil, which can promote SOM formation. The negative relationship between SOM and tree density is possibly due to differences in land use systems among sites with different tree densities. Sites with higher tree densities were mine abandoned sites, which were previously intensively disturbed and had a shorter time for vegetation recovery compared to other sites. Therefore, these sites had lower SOM compared to sites that were historically used for livestock grazing. The relationship between SOM and tree density was no longer significant after logarithmic transformation, indicating that this relationship might be driven by the differences in land use history among sites with different tree densities. The non-significant relationship between SOM and tree basal area, litter, soil moisture content and soil temperature suggests that these factors were not important in controlling SOM variability in this study. The result from this study suggests that in order to increase SOM in degraded miombo woodland, it is important to focus on CWD retention and prevention of soil erosion. Reforestation with multi-stemmed miombo species that promote CWD production and have dense canopy that can reduce soil erosion should be considered.

Here, we show that, in addition to the expected increase in aboveground live biomass, the carbon benefits of tropical forest conservation and management interventions may include a significant increase in the stock of dead wood, which is currently not considered in most carbon stock assessments. We also show that the increase in above- and belowground live biomass and dead wood may lead to a substantial rise in the total forest carbon stock that is 3–4 times larger than the increase in aboveground live biomass stock alone. Our results emphasize that carbon sequestration potential in African tropical forests may be substantially higher than previously thought and that there are significant co-benefits associated with interventions aimed at reducing deforestation and forest degradation. These include conservation and sustainable management of forests, which are essential for maintaining and improving the quality of freshwater and regulating water flow across the continent (i.e., the construction and maintenance of dams has led to the formation of numerous artificial lakes that, although initially created for power generation, are now being used for fishing and recreation), and the maintenance of wetlands that play a crucial role in supporting local livelihoods, such as small-scale agriculture, hunting, gathering, and aquaculture. These benefits may be achieved without compromising the production of timber and other forest products that are essential for local livelihoods and income, as well as for national and regional economic growth. We also show that the potential for carbon stock increases in African tropical forests is enormous and that even when considering the carbon stock in soils, which has not been included in this study, the region could still accumulate a substantial amount of carbon if forest cover is maintained and enhanced.

(Credit: Jason B. Houston/University of Florida)

Soils in areas of Zambia that were previously forested and have been cleared for agriculture have a higher concentration of organic matter than soils in areas that have never been forested, according to a new study.

The finding runs counter to the popular theory that once forests are cleared, the land will continue to degrade.

“This study shows that land that was previously forested in this part of the world still has a lot of potential,” said lead study author Jason B. Houston, a research scientist at the University of Florida’s School of Forest Resources and Conservation. “Even after it has been cleared and converted to another land use, it still has the potential to support a lot of biomass and a lot of production.”

The study is published in Biorgeosciences, an American Geophysical Union journal.

The finding is based on data Houston and fellow researchers collected while conducting a literature review on soil organic carbon (SOC) in Africa. The team looked at 304 studies from 42 different countries that included SOC data. The researchers found 65 studies from 23 African countries that met their criteria. Of those 65 studies, 14 were from Zambia.

The researchers found that, on average, soils in areas that had been previously forested in Zambia had 14.9 percent SOC in the top 20 centimeters of soil, compared to 12.2 percent SOC in areas that had never been forested.

The difference may seem small, but the higher the SOC, the better the soil quality. A higher SOC means the soil has more nutrients and moisture, which are necessary for supporting plant growth.

Soils with a higher concentration of organic matter are more productive and have better soil physical and chemical properties than soils with less organic matter, according to the study.

The higher SOC in the soils that were previously forested “is a testament to the fact that even though these forests were cleared, the amount of organic matter still remains in the soil,” Houston said.

The study notes that the topsoil in the areas that were previously forested “is of sufficiently high quality to support high levels of productivity if it were to be restored to forest.”

The results highlight the importance of not clearing forests, Houston said.

The researchers used the methods to assess the soil quality at three sites in Zambia, including a pine and eucalypt plantation, a eucalypt plantation and natural forest, and a conservation area with natural forest.

The results showed that the depth to which soil quality should be assessed depends on site conditions. At sites with deep soils and low natural fertility, such as the conservation site, they found that assessing soil quality to a depth of 150 centimetres was adequate. At sites with shallower soils and high natural fertility — such as the plantation sites — assessing soil quality to a depth of 70 centimetres was sufficient.

The researchers then compared the results with those from a similar study in South Africa, and found that in both countries, more than 70 per cent of soil quality variables considered good or very good at the start of the study remained good or very good at the end of the study. But at the Zambia sites, soil quality was significantly greater than at the South African sites.

The researchers said that the results suggest that the plantations in Zambia are being managed more effectively than similar plantations in South Africa, probably because the Zambia plantations are on relatively new land that has not been overworked.

The Platform is a forum for sharing knowledge and experience in chickpea research and development, and for identifying research needs and priorities. The Platform activities are implemented through the National Agricultural Research Systems (NARS) of Kenya, Ethiopia and India.

The Platform has been instrumental in bringing together stakeholders in the chickpea value chain in East and Southern Africa, and in promoting and facilitating the adoption of improved technologies and management practices through various activities. These include: a) a multi-stakeholder platform that meets twice a year to share information and experiences on research and development activities, challenges and opportunities in the region; b) a number of training and demonstration events to build capacity of stakeholders on improved technologies and practices; c) a number of on-station and on-farm demonstrations of improved cultivars and associated technologies; d) several field days to show-case research results and promote technology adoption; e) a number of dissemination workshops to pass on information on research results to a larger group of stakeholders; f) a number of study tours for stakeholders to see research activities and results at different research stations in Kenya, Ethiopia and India; g) participation in a number of national and international meetings, exhibitions and fairs to promote chickpea research and development in the region; and h) development of country-specific fact sheets to popularize technologies and pass on information on research activities and results to a larger group of stakeholders.

samples.ref: ኢትዮጵያ የሽምብራ ምርትን እንዴት እንዳሳደገች
samples.hyp:
Chickpeas are an important source of protein, fibre and micronutrients, including iron, zinc, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, and B vitamins. They have been shown to reduce the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and some cancers. 

The crop is also known to improve the nutritional quality of the diet, help manage blood sugar levels, and promote a healthy gut microbiome. 

With global chickpea production averaging 23.4 million tonnes per year, according to 2017 data from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the Middle East accounts for 60% of global consumption, followed by Asia with 22% and Africa with 6%. 

Traditionally, the highest concentrations of chickpea consumption are found in Middle Eastern and South Asian countries, where the crop is a staple part of the diet, but in recent years Africa has begun to play an increasingly important role as a chickpea-growing continent. 


According to the International Centre for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), Africa is the only continent where chickpea consumption is growing, with annual increases of 6% over the last decade. 


The majority of chickpeas produced in Africa come from Ethiopia. In 2016, Ethiopia produced 92% of Africa’s chickpeas and 4% of the world’s, with a national average of 0.8 tonnes per hectare. This is the highest national average yield in the world, and is a remarkable feat considering the country only began to widely cultivate the crop in the 1950s. 

The crop was introduced to Ethiopia in the 1940s as a drought-resistant food security crop for the country’s arid and semi-arid regions. However, it wasn’t until the 1980s that its cultivation started to increase due to a combination of factors, including the negative effects of drought, a rise in human population, in particular in rural areas, and a growing need for additional sources of protein and income. 

In the 1990s, the Ethiopian government began to implement new agricultural policies that encouraged the cultivation of new crops, such as chickpeas. This, in combination with improved farming practices and increased access to markets, contributed to the growth of the country’s chickpea sector, which has since then remained strong and stable. 

According to the 2016 FAO statistics, Ethiopia’s chickpea production has increased by 400% over the last 20 years.

The project also helped to establish a chickpea seed industry in Ethiopia, and helped train plant breeders and agronomists at the International Livestock Research Institute’s (ILRI) Addis Ababa office. This led to the release of several new chickpea varieties, and a doubling of the area of land cultivated with improved chickpeas between 1995 and 2018.

The researchers also found that the project’s investments in research and training had a high return on investment, with a cost of $443 per ton of seeds produced compared with a total value of $1,717 per ton of seeds sold, leading to a financial return of $1.27 for every $1 invested.

The project was a partnership between the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR), the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), and the World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF) and was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

The study, published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, is titled “Assessing the impacts, outcomes and returns on investment of a public–private partnership for agricultural research and development in Ethiopia: The case of the Ethiopian chickpea improvement program (2002–2018).”

Farmers in Kenya are also facing high levels of pests and diseases, which reduces the quantity and quality of their produce. Poor agricultural statistics are also hampering the development of the sector.

“[Poor agricultural statistics] make it difficult to make informed decisions on the best use of limited resources,” said Peter Nyuguto, Deputy Director General of the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics. “This is because most of the evidence we use to inform policy decisions are based on these statistics.”

The initiative is in line with the Comprehensive Africa Agriculture Development Program, which aims to improve the productivity of the agricultural sector, food security, and resilience in the face of climate change.

The initiative will focus on six areas to strengthen the production and dissemination of agricultural statistics in Kenya. These include developing a national strategy for agricultural statistics, strengthening the capacity of institutions that produce agricultural statistics, and improving the collection, production, and dissemination of quality statistics.

The initiative will also focus on modernizing the agricultural census and survey platforms, and the establishment of a multi-stakeholder platform to provide a forum for stakeholders in the sector to discuss issues related to agricultural statistics.

The initiative will be implemented over a four-year period at a cost of US$2.4 million. The Government of Kenya is contributing US$24,000 towards the implementation of the initiative.

The A.23.1 NTD deletion and RBD insertion result in a conformational change that increases the binding affinity of the spike for the human ACE2 receptor. Here we show that the A.23.1 spike protein has a higher binding affinity for human ACE2 than the wild-type (WT) or Alpha or Delta variant spikes. The A.23.1 spike also has a higher binding affinity for the Uganda monkey ACE2 than the WT or Beta variant spikes. The higher binding affinity of the A.23.1 spike for both human and monkey ACE2 is likely responsible for the increased transmissibility and high attack rate of the A.23.1 variant in Uganda. The higher binding affinity of the A.23.1 spike for human ACE2 also contributes to the increased severity of infection in the current Uganda epidemic. Our results highlight the importance of monitoring SARS-CoV-2 spike evolution and its impact on viral pathogenesis and pandemic control.

Uganda is a landlocked country in East Africa with a population of ~48 million people. It is a low-income country with a high burden of pre-existing co-infections including HIV, TB, and malaria. The country has a robust public health laboratory network with a national laboratory that performs molecular testing for COVID-19. Here, we describe the establishment of genomic surveillance for SARS-CoV-2 in Uganda and present the analysis of nearly 800 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Uganda, representing a 22-fold increase in the number of SARS-CoV-2 genomes from the continent of Africa. The majority of the virus genomes were obtained from patients with severe COVID-19 outcomes. We observed an overall genetic relatedness among the virus genomes from Uganda with other African sequences, but also observed close genetic relatedness to viruses from Europe and the United States. Overall, our results indicate that the virus that initially entered Uganda was from a West African lineage that is closely related to the virus from Europe and the United States. However, the majority of the virus genomes from Uganda are part of a more recent Uganda lineage that has also been detected in Kenya. These results were made possible by the collaboration between national public health laboratories in Uganda and Kenya and the global SARS-CoV-2 genomic surveillance network led by the Global Virome Project and Beijing Genomics Institute (BGI). The virus surveillance in Uganda is ongoing and has provided valuable information that has guided the response to the pandemic in Uganda. The information gained on the dynamics of virus spread and movement will continue to be important as Uganda and the world prepare for the next phase of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.

samples.hyp:
Source: Science X Network

The Alpha and Delta variants of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, have been dominant in many countries since early 2021. In Uganda, however, the third wave of COVID-19 infections was caused primarily by the Eta variant, which was first identified in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in June 2021. The Eta variant is also known as B.1.616.2. Researchers from Uganda and the U.S. have now sequenced and analyzed several Eta variant genomes to find out how this variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus has evolved in Uganda. They report their findings in the journal Viruses.

The study reveals that the Eta variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus has been circulating in Uganda since July 2021, several months before it was first detected in the country. The researchers also found that the Eta variant has several mutations that distinguish it from other SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern, including Alpha and Delta. The most prominent mutation in the Eta variant is the deletion of two amino acids at the spike protein's furin cleavage site, which the authors believe can increase the virus' transmissibility.

The authors also conducted a structural analysis of the Eta variant's spike protein and found that this variant contains several mutations that distinguish it from other SARS-CoV-2 variants. Four of these mutations are located in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the spike protein. Two of these RBD mutations have been linked to escape from neutralizing antibodies.

The authors note that the Eta variant contains four mutations that are of concern. These mutations affect the spike protein, which helps the virus enter human cells; the nucleocapsid protein, which helps package the virus' genetic material; and the ORF7a protein, which plays a role in viral infection.

More information: Hugues Anokute, et al. Molecular Characterization of SARS-CoV-2 B.1.616.2 (Eta) Variant in Uganda, Viruses (2022). DOI: 10.3390/v12020084

The good news is that several companies are monitoring the evolution of the coronavirus and have already started to adjust their vaccines accordingly.

For example, Pfizer and BioNTech recently announced that they are studying the impact of the South African variant on their vaccine. They are also developing a new version of their vaccine that specifically targets the South African variant.

Moderna is also evaluating the effectiveness of its vaccine against the South African variant.

In addition to monitoring the evolution of the virus, companies are also studying how people respond to different variants.

For example, some people may develop more antibodies or a stronger immune response after being vaccinated against one variant than another.

This information could be used to improve the effectiveness of vaccines in the future.

“Vaccine evasion is a serious problem for COVID-19,” said study senior author Dr. Kristian Andersen, a researcher at Scripps Research. “Our work highlights the ongoing need to develop new vaccine candidates that can keep up with the rapid evolution of SARS-CoV-2.”

The new study was co-authored by Andersen; Dr. Jesse Bloom, a researcher at Fred Hutchinson Cancer Alliance; and 10 other scientists at Scripps Research, the University of Washington, and the Allen Institute for AI.

The researchers began by analyzing the 13,226 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from around the world that had been sequenced and shared by global health authorities as of February 9, 2021. From this collection, the researchers identified 75 amino acid changes that were present in multiple samples and therefore likely to have been in the original virus that sparked the pandemic. The researchers then created a computer model of the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 genome and used it to simulate how the virus would have evolved over time in the absence of selective pressures like vaccines and drugs.

The model suggested that several key parts of the virus would have already mutated, including the spike protein, which the virus uses to enter cells and is the main target of most current vaccines.

“The fact that so many mutations have already occurred in the parts of the virus that are most important for its interaction with our bodies suggests that the virus is adapting to us, and that our immune systems are not yet fully prepared for this adaptation,” Andersen said.

Next, the researchers compared the ancestral virus simulations to 55,245 later genomes that had been sequenced as of February 9. They found that 98.4% of the later genomes showed at least one of the 75 ancestral mutations that they were looking for, and 88.6% showed 50 or more of these mutations. (The rest showed fewer mutations because they were sampled too late in the pandemic to avoid some of the more recent mutations, or because their genetic sequences were incomplete or too closely matched to other genomes to make reliable comparisons.)

The researchers then applied machine learning to ask whether the later genomes showed evidence of natural selection. Specifically, they asked whether the virus had shifted its composition in specific ways that provided it with an advantage in transmission between people. They found evidence that selection had acted on 32 out of the 75 ancestral mutations, with a particularly strong effect on four mutations.

A Review of the Literature on Female Embodiment and Identity Construction in the Ancient Near East

The ancient Near East is a rich but difficult region for the study of women. On the one hand, women are frequently mentioned in the sources, which attests to their relative visibility in society. On the other hand, the image of a woman is often reduced to her sexual characteristics, which attests to the limitations of her visibility. This article reviews the recent literature on female embodiment and identity construction in the ancient Near East. The analysis focuses on the different strategies used by women and men to represent women’s bodies and identities, and reveals a social and cultural tension between the androcentric discourse that tends to reduce women to their sexual characteristics and the alternative discourse that tends to enlarge women’s social and cultural roles. The article argues that the female body and identity were at stake in the ancient Near East, as they are nowadays, in a constant struggle for power.

The ancient Near East is a fascinating region for the study of women. Keywords: female genital mutilation/cutting, FGM/C, Indonesia, Ethiopia, Kenya, case studies, socio-cultural factors, legal factors, health factors, prevalence, practice, reasons, circumstances
Abstract: Female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) is a collective name for all procedures that involve altering or injuring the female external genitalia for non-medical reasons. The practice is embedded in the social and cultural structures of communities worldwide, and diverse social, cultural, legal and health factors influence the prevalence of FGM/C. This article presents three case studies that aim to better understand the reasons for and circumstances of FGM/C among girls and women in three countries in Asia and Africa, Indonesia, Ethiopia and Kenya, that have a high prevalence of FGM/C. The case studies are based on a literature review and secondary data analysis and were conducted within the framework of the UN Joint Programme on FGM/C. The three countries represent different socio-legal contexts, in which FGM/C is practiced at different prevalence levels. In Indonesia, FGM/C is practiced by Muslim and non-Muslim communities at high prevalence levels, in Ethiopia it is a centuries-old practice among the Circassian communities, and in Kenya it is performed on young girls from various ethnic groups at lower prevalence levels than in Ethiopia and Indonesia. The case studies identify factors that influence the prevalence of FGM/C within the different contexts and show that FGM/C is a product of complex social and cultural factors and is strongly influenced by social interactions. The authors argue that addressing the diverse socio-cultural, legal and health context factors of FGM/C is key to successfully implementing programmes and interventions aimed at reducing FGM/C. The case studies highlight the importance of in-depth understanding of the local context and the need to collect community-specific data to inform the design and implementation of effective programmes to end FGM/C. samples.src: This study was a collaboration between scientists from Ethiopia, Indonesia and the Netherlands, and forms part of a bigger project, called the ‘Yes I Do programme’, whicht aims to reduce teen pregnancies, child marriage and FGM.
samples.ref: ይህ ጥናት በኢትዮጵያ፣ በኢንዶኔዥያ እና በኔዘርላንደስ ሳይንቲስቶች ትብብር የተሰራ ሲሆን ‘የስ አይ ዱ ፕሮግራም’ የሚባል በጉርምስና ጊዜ የሚከሰቱ እርግዝናዎችን፣ የልጅነት ጋብቻን እና FGMን ለመቀነስ ያለመ ትልቅ ፕሮጀክት አካል ነው።
samples.hyp:
The programme is being implemented in Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda and Zambia. The ‘Yes I Do’ programme is a combination of a mass media campaign and community mobilisation. The mass media campaign includes TV and radio spots, billboards, and printed materials that are all targeted at young people. The community mobilisation component includes the training of community and religious leaders to talk about the importance of waiting with sex until they are older, and the dangers of early pregnancy and marriage. This component also trains these leaders to support young people in setting their own goals for the future, and to encourage them to achieve their goals through staying in school and avoiding early pregnancy and marriage. The mass media campaign and community mobilisation are based on information obtained from focus group discussions and individual interviews with young people, parents, community leaders and religious leaders. The aim of the current study was to gain more insight into the effects of the ‘Yes I Do’ programme, by determining whether the programme changed the knowledge, attitudes and behaviour of young people with regard to preventing early pregnancy and marriage.

samples.src: Reproductive Hormones Imbalance, Germ Cell Apoptosis, Abnormal Sperm Morphophenotypes and Ultrastructural Changes in Testis of African Giant Rats (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Exposed to Sodium Metavanadate Intoxication
samples.ref: ለሶዲየም ሜታቫናዴት መመረዝ ለተጋለጡ የአፍሪካ ግዙፍ አይጦች የመራቢያ ሆርሞኖች አለመመጣጠን፣ የጀርም ህዋስ ሂደታዊ የህዋስ ሞት፣ ያልተለመዱ የወንዴ ዘር ክስት ባህሪያት እና ቅርጾች እንዲሁም በወንዴ ዘር እጢ ውስጥ ያሉ አልትራ መዋቅራዊ ለውጦች (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840)
samples.hyp:
The study was conducted to evaluate the effects of sodium metavanadate (NaMO) on reproductive hormones, germ cell apoptosis, sperm morphology and ultrastructure of testis in male African giant rats. Twenty-one rats were randomly divided into three groups: the first group (n=7) served as control, the second group (n=7) was administered NaMO at a dose of 10 mg/kg body weight, and the third group (n=7) was administered NaMO at a dose of 20 mg/kg body weight for 60 days. Blood samples were collected from all animals at the end of the experiment, and the levels of testosterone, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) were measured. Testis were removed, prepared for histological and ultrastructural studies, and examined for apoptosis using the TUNEL technique. Sperm morphology was evaluated by the standard method. Results showed a significant decrease in body weight of rats treated with both doses of NaMO. Testicular weights of rats treated with 20 mg/kg NaMO were significantly lower than those of the control group and the group treated with 10 mg/kg NaMO. Testicular histology showed that NaMO caused testicular degeneration and atrophy. The apoptotic index (AI) in the testis of rats treated with 20 mg/kg NaMO was significantly higher than that in the control group and the group treated with 10 mg/kg NaMO. The percentage of abnormal sperm was significantly increased in both treated groups compared to the control group, and this increase was more pronounced in the group treated with 20 mg/kg NaMO. Ultrastructural changes were observed in the testis of rats treated with NaMO including the appearance of vacuoles in the cytoplasm of some germ cells, detachment of the germ cells from the spermatogonia/spermatocytes, disruption of the blood-testis barrier, and accumulation of apoptotic bodies in the lumen of the seminiferous tubules. In conclusion, NaMO caused a significant decrease in body weight of rats and testicular weight, atrophy and vacuolization of testicular tissue, disruption of the blood-testis barrier, and an increase in the percentage of abnormal sperm. The AI in the testis was increased, and ultrastructural changes were observed in the testis of rats treated with NaMO.

samples.ref: በቅርብ ጊዜ አካባቢያዊ የቫናዲየም መጋለጥ እየጨመረ መጥቷል።
samples.hyp:
This is due to the increase in vanadium mining and processing activities. Vanadium is a metal that is used as an additive in many consumer products such as ceramics, catalysts, alloys, and lubricants. The aim of this study was to assess the level of urinary vanadium among workers in a vanadium processing industry in South Africa. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 293 workers in the vanadium processing industry in South Africa. The study population consisted of workers who were 18 years and older. Overall, 51.2% of the workers were found to be exposed to urinary vanadium. The exposed group had a significantly higher mean urinary vanadium excretion rate than the unexposed group (P < 0.001). There was a significant positive correlation between urinary vanadium and work experience (P = 0.013). The present study showed that a significant number of the workers in the vanadium processing industry were exposed to elevated levels of urinary vanadium. The exposed workers had a significantly higher mean urinary vanadium excretion rate than the unexposed workers. The level of urinary vanadium increased with an increase in work experience. Although the level of urinary vanadium among the study participants was within the reference value, it is important to continually monitor the level of vanadium among workers in the vanadium processing industry due to the toxic effects that vanadium has on health.

It is also an essential nutrient, and 100% of dietary intake is absorbed in healthy individuals. The majority of dietary intake comes from fish, shellfish and seafood. The general population is at low risk for Hg exposure, but women of childbearing age and pregnant women are at increased risk due to cumulative and/or developmental effects. Once absorbed, Hg is distributed rapidly to all organs and tissues, including the brain. The primary route of exposure for the general population is via the diet. Other sources include dental amalgam, vaccines containing thimerosal and dermal exposure to Hg compounds in some industrial work settings. Once inside the body, Hg is methylated by an enzyme to form methylmercury (MeHg), the most toxic and potentially neurotoxic form. MeHg exposure can be reduced by avoiding consumption of certain types of fish. EPA has developed fish advisories for water bodies where Hg contamination may exceed advisory levels. EPA and other agencies have also set maximum contaminant levels (MCLs) for Hg in drinking water. Because of the potential for adverse neurodevelopment in children from in utero exposure, EPA is in the process of developing an advisory for Hg in soil.

samples.src: The current study was conducted to investigate the reproductive toxicity of sodium metavanadate (SMV) in male African giant rats.
samples.ref: የአሁኑ ጥናት የተካሄደው የሶዲየም ሜታቫናዴት (ሶ.ሜ.ቫ) የመራቢያ መርዛማነትን በአፍሪካ ግዙፍ ወንድ አይጦች ላይ ለመመርመር ነው።
samples.hyp:
SMV is an industrial chemical used in the production of ceramics, catalysts, and refractory materials. It is also used in the production of fireworks and in the laboratory as a reducing agent. SMV is reported to have genotoxic effects in several animal species. However, there is a lack of information on the reproductive toxicity of SMV in non-rodent species. The present study evaluated the effects of SMV exposure on reproductive parameters, testosterone, and sperm characteristics in male African giant rats. A total of 24 male rats were randomly assigned to four groups. Group I served as the control group, while Groups II, III, and IV were treated with SMV at 50, 100, and 150 mg/kg body weight, respectively, once daily for ninety days. Following the experimental period, blood samples were collected for the determination of testosterone and sperm parameters. Results showed that SMV significantly (p<0.05) decreased body weight of the rats at 100 and 150 mg/kg doses. Testicular weights were significantly reduced in all treated groups. SMV exposure also resulted in a significant (p<0.05) decrease in the sperm motility and percentage of progressively motile sperm at all tested doses. The percentage of non-motile sperm was significantly (p<0.05) increased in all treated groups. SMV exposure at the doses used in the present study resulted in a significant (p<0.05) decrease in the testosterone level at 100 and 150 mg/kg doses. In conclusion, the present study indicates that exposure to SMV at 100 and 150 mg/kg produces adverse effects on sperm quality and testosterone in male African giant rats.

The highest level of tungsten was found in the yellow croaker fish, which is commonly eaten in the delta region. The researchers also found that the higher the level of tungsten in the fish, the higher the level of a protein called tungsten (WTS) in their muscles. WTS has been shown to be toxic to fish and can change the physical properties of fish meat. "Our results indicate that the Pearl River is contaminated with tungsten, and the main source of tungsten is likely the high tungsten content in cement used in construction sites along the river," said study lead author Dr. Chear Yen Chew from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in the press release. "Since tungsten is known to be toxic to fish, and our results show that the local fish have developed a defense mechanism by inducing the production of WTS to fight off the toxic metal, we suggest that further research be conducted to find out if tungsten is a potential health risk to human beings as well," he added.

Tungsten is used in many industries as a construction material and in the production of chemicals and fuel. It is also used in the production of many household items such as light bulbs, radios, television tubes, and x-ray tubes. The scientists warn that the widespread use of tungsten in industry could have serious environmental consequences. "The widespread use of tungsten in industry has led to its presence in the environment and our food chain, and our study is a wake-up call that more research is needed to understand the environmental impact of tungsten," said co-author Dr. Stella Asgedom from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

The main objective of this study was to assess the floristic composition of homegardens in the district. Data were collected from 48 homegardens in 8 villages of Gozamin district. The floristic composition of homegardens was characterized using Shannon-Wiener diversity index, Simpson dominance index, and Renkl’s quotient. The results showed that homegarden owners in the study area planted 55 plant species from 25 families. The families Poaceae, Rosaceae, and Fabaceae contributed the most to the floristic diversity of homegardens. The Shannon-Wiener diversity index, Simpson dominance index, and Renkl’s quotient values were 2.89, 0.61, and 0.52, respectively. The results of cluster analysis revealed that the floristic composition of homegardens in the study area were characterized by four plant families: Poaceae, Rosaceae, Fabaceae, and Rubiaceae. The results of this study provide baseline information for future research on homegarden agrobiodiversity in the study area, and may contribute to the conservation and sustainable use of homegarden flora in the study area.

In this study, we aimed to identify the main factors that influence the management of homegardens by the Bribri and Cabecar indigenous groups in Talamanca, Costa Rica. We conducted semi-structured interviews to 48 community members of two different homegarden management systems: one based on private property and the other on collective management. We analyzed the influence of sociodemographic factors, as well as the importance of some variables related to the perception of the participants regarding the use and management of natural resources. Our results show that the most important factors influencing homegarden management are related to the perception of the participants regarding the management of natural resources. Participants from the private property system stated that the main reasons for managing their homegardens were to provide food security, to earn money by selling surplus production, and to manage natural resources in a sustainable way. In contrast, participants from the collective system stated that the main purpose of their homegardens was to provide food security. I

n addition, participants from the collective system perceived that the use of some species of plants in their homegardens had negative consequences for the conservation of biodiversity, while those from the private property system considered that the sale of surplus production generates a better distribution of income at the community level. This is the first time that the influence of the perception of natural resources management on the management of homegardens by two indigenous groups in Talamanca, Costa Rica is evaluated. Our results show that the management of natural resources is influenced in different ways depending on the sociodemographic characteristics of the participants and the homegarden management system. Therefore, in order to design efficient conservation strategies, it is essential to consider the particular cultural knowledge of the local communities and to take into account the particular conditions of each place.

samples.ref: የኢትዮጵያ የቤት አትክልቶች የምግብ ደህንነትን እና አጠባበቅን ይደግፋሉ።
samples.hyp:
Gardens in Ethiopia are a vital source of food and income for many rural families, and play a crucial role in conserving the country’s biodiversity. This is according to a new study led by the University of British Columbia (UBC) and the Norwegian University of Life Sciences, which is the first to examine the role of home gardens in the food security and conservation of 25 major crops in Ethiopia. The study was published today in the journal PLOS ONE.

“We found that home gardens are a significant source of food and income for rural Ethiopian families, particularly during times of crisis,” said lead author Corrine Muller, a recent UBC graduate who completed the study as part of her Master’s research in the UBC School of Community and Regional Planning.

“Gardens also play a vital role in conserving the biodiversity of many Ethiopian plants, some of which are in danger of going extinct,” added Muller, who completed the study as part of the UBC Food Systems and Climate Change Initiative in collaboration with the Institute of Development and International Relations (IDRI) in Addis Ababa.

Home gardens – which the researchers define as small-scale, diverse food and cash production systems located on the residence plot immediately surrounding a household – are a common feature of Ethiopian rural life. The study indicated that gardens were used by households to produce a variety of crops, including teff, orange, lemongrass, onion, chili pepper, and tomato.
